Each experiment compares infection in warmed mesocosms (the exposed group) with ambient controls (the control group). Experiment 1 has 100 individuals in each group, and Experiment 2 has 50.
We’ll cover the two main effect sizes for these data: the log odds ratio (lnOR) and the log risk ratio (lnRR)

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
These are among the most commonly used effect size types in meta-analyses. These effect sizes compare a continuous response variable between two discrete categorical predictors (e.g., Control vs Experiment). By continuous, we mean a measurement summarized by its central tendency (mean, median) and dispersion (variance, standard deviation, standard error) across replicates. These replicates are the sample size.
The primary effect sizes that can be calculated with this data are standardized mean difference (SMD) and log-transformed ratio of means (lnRoM). Please see here for a more thorough description of these effect sizes, their assumptions, and their interpretation. In general, the extraction for these effect sizes is similar. However, as you will see, some data types constrain you to only using SMD because of values ≤ 0 or because of model estimates (t statistics), which only SMD can handle.






Important



The primary aim of this tutorial is to align extractions with target estimands of SMD and lnRoM (see here).
However, some of the extraction challenges in this page are naturally suited for alternative estimands that account for different study designs. These alternative estimands are not interchangeable with meta-analyses focused on SMD or lnRoM. When these cases show up, we acknowledge the “ideal” estimands but present solutions to allow calculation of SMD and lnRoM target estimands. We also briefly discuss these alternative estimands in the escalc cheatsheet. If your entire meta-analysis consists of these situations, then you may want to use these alternative estimands directly.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
The simple cases
We’ll start with the simplest figure types, mostly in order to contrast with more complex types. If you’re using metaDigitise() to extract data (Pick et al. 2018), the function will guide you through calibrating the axes and selecting the top of the error bars and the top of the bars themselves (the mean). If the figure reports standard error (\(se\)), metaDigitise() will convert it automatically to standard deviation (\(sd\)). Always be aware of what the error type the figures (or text) are reporting.







Figure 1










NoteWatch out for misreporting of \(SE\) as \(SD\)



One challenging problem is when primary study authors misreport error types. Unfortunately, this is not uncommon and it can have a huge influence on your results.
After extracting all of your studies and converting the various forms of error (i.e., \(SE\), confidence intervals) to \(SD\), we recommend screening the \(CVs\) (\(CV = sd/m\)) of your dataset. Look for anomalously small values and double check the original articles from which those estimates were extracted. If in doubt, contact the authors and/or conduct sensitivity analyses excluding effect sizes with extremely low \(CV\).
You could also consider doing simulations of data on the primary study scale to see how likely it would be, given the sample size, to arrive at the reported \(SD\) values.


Box plots are also straightforward and involve extracting the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, and maximum values. metaDigitise() will walk you through that extraction and will automatically convert the interquartile range and median to mean±SD.






NoteConvert median ± interquartile range to mean ± sd





For a median \(m\), quartiles \(q_1\) and \(q_3\), and sample size \(n\), the conversion is:
\[\begin{aligned}
&\bar{x} \approx \frac{q_1+m+q_3}{3} \\
&sd \approx \frac{q_3-q_1}{2\Phi^{-1}\left(\frac{0.75n-0.125}{n+0.25}\right)} \\
\end{aligned}\]
where \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the inverse of the standard normal distribution function (qnorm() in R).










Figure 2




It’s also common to see figures like this with more complex non-independence structures. These can be dealt with by digitizing only the final time point or by controlling for non-independence with random effects (see here for a brief discussion of these issues).







Figure 3




Let’s move on to more complex situations.






Important3-dimensional plots



There was a brief unfortunate period in the 1990s when these became popular. 3D plots often depicted multivariate histograms, as well as other data types such as bar charts.
We won’t discuss these much here, we just want to acknowledge your pain if you come across one. Hopefully the general plot designs will be similar to those covered in this tutorial. We believe that WebPlotDigitizer has options to calibrate 3D plots. Alternatively, popular LLMs (e.g., Gemini or Claude or ChatGPT) are likely able to extract this data.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Histograms
It’s also common to see the outcome variable of the two discrete predictor groups plotted as separate histograms:







Figure 4




metaDigitise() luckily has built-in functionality for dealing with histograms. The function will guide you through each step, which requires calibrating the axes and then clicking on the left and right corners of each bar. It’ll then convert the extracted distributions into means±sd. This can be time-consuming. You can also try getting an LLM model to do it for you.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Violin and density plots
The beauty of modern plotting techniques has led to a proliferation of new ways to visualize data. Like violin plots.







Figure 5




Violin plots are basically a vertical version of a density plot:







Figure 6




A violin or density plot shows a smoothed estimate of the distribution, rather than the original observations. Its shape depends partly on plotting choices, especially how much smoothing was used. This means that the width of a violin cannot be read as a standard deviation, and the bumps should not be treated as individual observations.
The example below draws the same observations three times. Only the smoothing changes. The sample mean and SD are therefore identical in every panel, even though the distributions appear to have different shapes.







Figure 7— The same observations displayed using three different amounts of smoothing. Changing the plotting settings changes the apparent shape, but it does not change the observations, their mean, or their SD.




For an SMD or lnRoM, we recommend the following extraction order:

Look elsewhere first. Check the text, tables, figure caption, supplementary files, and data repository for the mean, SD, and sample size.
If individual observations are visible, digitize those observations. Calculate the mean and SD from the extracted values. Points may overlap, so use the reported sample size rather than counting the visible points whenever possible.
If the plot contains summary markers, extract only statistics that the caption or legend defines. A dot could represent either a mean or a median, and bars could represent an SD, interquartile range, or confidence interval. Their meaning should not be guessed from their appearance.
If only the violin or density outline is available, contact the authors. If the required statistics cannot be obtained, record the outcome as unavailable for calculating an SMD or lnRoM.







WarningDo not estimate the SD from the width of the violin



The outline is influenced by the smoothing method and bandwidth. Violin plots may also be scaled to have the same area or maximum width even when their sample sizes differ. The width therefore does not provide an SD or, unless the plotting method explicitly says otherwise, a sample size.


It is technically possible to digitize the outline at many outcome values and use its width to reconstruct the displayed density. We do not recommend this as a routine extraction method. The variance of the displayed density includes variation introduced by smoothing, so it is not necessarily the variance of the original observations. Recovering the original SD would require details such as the kernel, bandwidth, trimming, and any axis transformation, as well as a separately reported sample size. If such a reconstruction is attempted, label it as an estimated result, validate it against the plotted curve, and test whether excluding it changes the meta-analysis.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Proportion data (0-1) bounded without error
Sometimes SMD/lnRoM design types will present the total % of a population for a study design that is otherwise indistinguishable from other SMD/lnRoM studies in your dataset.
For an individual binary outcome coded 1 when the event occurs and 0 otherwise, the mean is the event proportion \(p\). Its variance and standard deviation are determined by \(p\):
\[\begin{aligned}
&m = p \\
&Var = p(1-p) \\
&sd = \sqrt{p(1-p)}. \\
\end{aligned}\]
The expected number of events among \(N_{total}\) individuals is \(pN_{total}\), but that count is not the mean of the individual 0/1 outcomes. These formulas describe individual binary observations; they do not give the standard deviation among site-level or trial-level proportions.
If you’re facing this type of data in your meta-analysis you may want to consider whether SMD/lnRoM are the correct effect sizes for your meta-analysis. This type of data is meant to be analyzed with an lnOR type effect size. Alternatively, if these are rare scenarios in your meta-analysis, you may also consider calculating lnOR from these data and converting the lnOR point estimate and sampling variance to SMD. See here for a tutorial on effect size conversions and their assumptions.
Note that these conversions constrain you to using SMD: it is not possible to convert lnOR to lnRoM.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Mean±sd proportion data (0-1)
Suppose a study reports a proportion, i.e., a binary response, for each independent site and then reports the mean and SD across sites. These observations cannot be less than 0 or greater than 1. The boundaries therefore constrain how much the observations can vary, and that constraint depends on the mean.
This mean–variance relationship can make comparisons on the original scale strongly heteroscedastic. To use 0-1 bounded data, you should transform your means and standard deviation to stretch values into an approximation of normality.






Note



Note that some data types in ecology may not be true proportions but have similar properties. For example, plant cover data is often 0-1 bounded depending on how it’s calculated (though often reported on 0-100 scale). Flag these for correction following the code below.


The arcsine-square-root transformation does this (Macartney et al. 2022):
\[
g(x)=\arcsin(\sqrt{x}).
\]
The transformation stretches values near 0 and 1 more than values near 0.5. If the individual proportions are available, transform each observation and then calculate the transformed mean and SD directly. If only the original mean \(m\) and SD \(sd\) are reported, the delta method provides the following approximation:
\[\begin{aligned}
&m' \approx \arcsin(\sqrt{m})\\
&sd' \approx \frac{sd}{2\sqrt{m(1-m)}}.\\
\end{aligned}\]
The denominator becomes smaller near 0 or 1, so the transformation expands an original-scale SD near a boundary more than an equally sized SD near 0.5. This reduces some of the mechanical dependence between the mean and the available variance.
In R:

m = 0.7
sd = 0.1

m_trans <- asin(sqrt(m))
sd_trans <- sd / (2 * sqrt(m * (1 - m)))

c("transformed_mean" = m_trans, "transformed_sd" = sd_trans)

transformed_mean   transformed_sd 
       0.9911566        0.1091089 


This is only a local approximation. In general, transforming a reported mean does not give exactly the same answer as averaging the transformed observations, and the approximated \(sd'\) does not necessarily equal their transformed SD. The approximation can be poor when the mean is very close to 0 or 1 or when the observations are widely dispersed. It is undefined when \(m\) is exactly 0 or 1.
When the approximation is appropriate, an SMD can be calculated from the transformed means and SDs and interpreted as a standardized contrast on the transformed scale. The sample size remains the number of independent sites, plots, or trials represented by the reported SD.
Do not use the transformed means to calculate an lnRoM and interpret it as a proportional change on the original scale. The arcsine transformation changes the ratio between values.
Unfold the section below if you want to see a full demonstration of the relationship between means and standard deviation in proportion data:






Note





For a proportion \(X\) with population mean \(\mu\), the population variance cannot exceed:
\[
Var(X) \leq \mu(1-\mu).
\]
The largest possible population SD is therefore \(\sqrt{\mu(1-\mu)}\). It is largest when the mean is 0.5 and approaches zero as the mean approaches either boundary. For example, the maximum population SD is 0.50 when the mean is 0.50, but only about 0.22 when the mean is 0.05 or 0.95. A group with a mean near a boundary simply has less room to vary on the original scale.







Figure 8— The possible population SD of an outcome bounded between 0 and 1 depends on its mean. The blue region contains possible combinations; the dark curve is the maximum SD, not the expected SD.




The curve is an upper boundary, not a formula for estimating a missing SD. Binary observations coded 0 and 1 reach this boundary because their variance is exactly \(p(1-p)\). Proportions measured across sites, plots, or trials can have any SD below the boundary. Their actual variation also depends on factors such as the number of individuals contributing to each proportion, differences among sites, and clustering.






Note



The figure shows the population relationship. A reported sample SD usually uses \(n-1\) in its denominator. Its corresponding finite-sample bound is \(sd^2 \leq [n/(n-1)]m(1-m)\), so a sample SD can sit slightly above the curve, especially when the number of independent units is small.











CautionBinary counts and summarized proportions



If a paper reports an exact event count and denominator, such as 17 survivors among 25 animals, those values can be entered directly into an lnOR or lnRR calculation. If the rest of your meta-analysis is of SMD/lnRoM type data, you can convert the calculated lnOR effect size to SMD (but not to lnRoM). See our converting effect sizes page.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Differences
Some studies used paired designs where, instead of reporting each pair separately, they subtract the paired samples from each other and report mean±error of the difference.







Figure 9— Boxplot of paired differences (treatment minus control) for 15 simulated pairs. The box shows the interquartile range and the line shows the median.




To calculate our target estimand of SMD or lnRoM with this data, we can extract the difference from the boxplot, and convert the medians and interquartile ranges to means±sd. This dataset would look like this:


\(mean_{difference}\)
\(sd_{difference}\)


5.7138734
0.9071623


To calculate SMD (which is necessary because we are no longer dealing with ratio-scale data and negative values are likely), we have to be creative.

Set the mean difference to either the control or experimental group, depending on the direction of the rest of your dataset (e.g., positive or negative). Set the other mean to 0.
Use \(sd_{difference}\) for both the control and the experimental group.

As such your data will look like this:








\(mean_{control}\)
\(sd_{control}\)
\(mean_{experiment}\)
\(sd_{experiment}\)


5.71
0.91
0
0.91


Since the data is paired, you should use a paired version of SMD to calculate your effect sizes.
In metafor::escalc, this would be measure = "SMCRP".

escalc(measure = "SMCRP",
       data = diff_dt,
       m1i = mean_control, 
       m2i = mean_experiment,
       sd1i = sd_control, 
       sd2i = sd_experiment,
       ri = 0.5,
       ni = 15)


  mean_control sd_control mean_experiment sd_experiment     yi     vi 
1     5.713873  0.9071623               0     0.9071623 6.0849 0.8381 


“SMCRP” is comparable to unpaired SMD estimators and so can be included in your main analysis. However, cases like this should be flagged for sensitivity analysis.






NoteAlternative estimand: Standardized Mean Change



The example above is ideally suited for a different estimand: standardized mean change. Unfortunately, this estimand is not comparable to SMD. Thus only use this estimand if all of your data consists of differences between groups.
In metafor::escalc, this estimand can be calculated with measure = "SMCC":

escalc(measure = "SMCC",
       m1i = -8.11, m2i = 0,
       sd1i = 1.27, sd2i = 0,
       ri = 0.5,
       ni = 15)

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
section: Ratios of control and treatment groups
text:
Ratios of control and treatment groups
Some studies report a response ratio directly. Before extracting it, determine how it was calculated. Two similar-looking summaries estimate different quantities.
If the ratio is of two group means (\(\bar{x}\):
\[
RR_{means}=\frac{\bar{x}_{treatment}}{\bar{x}_{control}}.
\] Its natural logarithm is the usual lnRoM point estimate. To calculate its usual sampling variance, we still need information about the uncertainty of both group means and whether the groups were independent or paired. A single reported ratio without an SE, confidence interval, group SDs, or other usable uncertainty is not usable, unfortunately.
However, a study may instead calculate ratios at the observational-scale (\(x\)) between paired measurements. \[
RR_i=\frac{x_{treatment,i}}{x_{control,i}}.
\]
The mean of the individual ratios won’t be equal to the ratio of the group means. Likewise, the logarithm of the mean ratio is generally not equal to the mean of the logged ratios. To the best of our knowledge, this data is lost to the abyss.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
section: Results reported as an effect size itself
text:
Results reported as an effect size itself
A similar situation is when studies report their results as an effect size itself (e.g., SMD or lnRoM). These could be extracted directly as your effect size except that in our experience these studies rarely report a measure of dispersion (sampling variance, or SD or SE which could be converted to variance).
If a measure of error is reported then you can use these effect sizes directly or convert them to your target effect size. See here on how to convert between effect size types.
If a measurement of error is provided, then you can extract the data as is, and convert that error to sampling variance. For example, if SMD ± standard error was plotted, the sampling variance is \[vi = SE^2\].
If a study reports standardized mean differences (e.g., Cohen’s d), which is uncorrected estimator of SMD, you can use escalc to convert it to Hedges' g, the dominant estimator of SMD by specifying Cohen’s d with the di argument:

escalc(measure = "SMD",
       di = 5, 
       n1i = 10, n2i = 10)


      yi     vi 
1 4.7882 0.7732 


In many other cases, there’s nothing you can do but email the authors and hope they still have their raw data.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Before-after-control-impact designs
Before-after control-impact (BACI) designs are considered gold standard experimental designs. Yet most meta-analyses ignore the before treatment and only extract and analyze the ‘after’ treatments. Here is a BACI figure:







Figure 10— Mean and SD (error bars, ±1 SD) of simulated control and impact (treatment) sites before and after the treatment (n = 50 per group). Striped columns show values after the treatment.




In this case, only extracting and analyzing the ‘after’ data isn’t a big deal, because the differences in the ‘before’ groups in the control and treatment are minimal.
However, what about a more problematic result, where there’s a big difference in before conditions between the control and treatment?







Figure 11— The same design with a large difference between control and treatment before the treatment. Error bars show ±1 SD (n = 50 per group, simulated). The difference before the treatment persists after it.




You may also see time series, where the first measurement in the time series is before the treatment. This presents similar conundrums. In that case, it may seem like the easiest bet is just to ignore the before data but, if there were differences between treatments in the before step, this leads to similar problems.






Note



There are alternative estimands for this type of study design (Becker 1988; Morris 2008). If your meta-analysis only includes these study designs, then you should use them. See the escalc cheatsheet for the measure options. However, we expect that you are encountering this study design in a meta-analysis otherwise using standard SMD or lnRoM effect sizes.


If you decide to include studies like this, we believe that the best solution is to calculate the difference between the before and after group means and use the before treatment standard deviation in your calculations.
The extracted dataset would look like this:










mean_diff_control
sd_before_control
mean_diff_impact
sd_before_impact


4.337091
1.076947
5.575706
1.013183










Note



BACI designs often lead to negative values from subtracting the before treatment from the after treatments—which requires you to use SMD instead of lnRoM as your estimand.


You can also imagine that this data bears certain assumptions—especially from ignoring the after standard deviation. It might be acceptable to average the before and after standard deviations—we don’t know. Regardless, we recommend sensitivity analyses including and excluding this data and potentially using either averaged or before standard deviation to see if that changes results.
The final effect size can be calculated as normal:

escalc(measure = "SMD",
       m2i = mean_diff_control,
       sd2i = sd_after_control,
       m1i = mean_diff_impact,
       sd1i = sd_after_impact,
       n1i = 15,
       n2i = 15,
       data = dt_wide,
       append = FALSE)


      yi     vi 
1 1.4404 0.1679 


Note that you may wish to use a paired estimator for this if the control and impact groups were paired spatially (they cannot be paired temporally).
These 4 group designs may appear in other contexts than pre and post treatment and can be fairly in common in ecological field experiments. For example, to understand if reintroduced wild dogs indirectly affect vegetation by reducing dik-dik browsing and abundance, Ford et al. (2015) placed controls and exclosures in areas with and without wild dogs, predicting that the difference between controls and exclosures would be greatest where there are no wild dogs.







Figure 12— Simulated vegetation response (n = 15 plots per cell; error bars show ±1 SD) in controls and exclosures, with and without wild dogs. The values show the predicted pattern and are not data from Ford et al. (2015).




The same difference-in-differences logic above applies to this crossed design. The exclosure effect (exclosure minus control) is calculated within each wild dog level, and the difference between those effects is the interaction:

ford_wide <- dcast(ford_sum, wild_dogs ~ exclosure, value.var = "mean")
ford_wide[, exclosure_effect := Exclosure - Control]
ford_did <- ford_wide[wild_dogs == "Absent", exclosure_effect] -
  ford_wide[wild_dogs == "Present", exclosure_effect]
ford_wide

Key: <wild_dogs>
   wild_dogs  Control Exclosure exclosure_effect
      <char>    <num>     <num>            <num>
1:    Absent 4.252602  8.231620         3.979018
2:   Present 6.469387  6.687029         0.217642


The exclosure effect is 3.98 where wild dogs are absent and 0.22 where they are present, so the difference-in-differences is 3.76. A positive value matches the prediction that wild dogs influence the effects of dik diks on vegetation.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
% Change
Sometimes BACI type data is presented directly as percent change, which saves us some of the steps above.







Figure 13— Percent change from before to after the treatment for control and treatment groups. Values are illustrative, and error bars show ±5 percentage points.




In this case, use the percent change values directly to calculate SMD. You will not be able to use lnRoM in these cases because of negative values.
Because this data has been transformed into a percent, if this percent is bounded between 0 and 100, you may have to convert it to a proportion (divide by 100) and arcsin transform it to reduce boundary issues. See above for further discussion of this transformation.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Discrete x discrete crossed design
Sometimes you are interested explicitly in interactions between two treatments. In most studies one of the treatments you are interested in would otherwise be a moderator (e.g., not crossed with the main experimental comparison), however in others you find a fully crossed design.







Figure 14— Crossed design: the outcome before and after the treatment (x-axis) for two levels of factor 2 (plain or striped columns). Error bars show ±1 SD; n = 50 per group (simulated).




In these cases, you’ll need to record these crossed moderators in separate columns in your dataset. If your meta-analysis is explicitly interested in those moderators, you’ve scored a major win! If not, then these crossed moderators can be ignored (but should be factored into the non-independence variables in your dataset accordingly).

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Continuous x discrete crossed design
However, sometimes interactions will be between continuous and discrete variables:







Figure 15— Simulated outcome against a continuous variable for the control group (left) and the treatment group (right). Each point is one observation (10 per group); no error bars are shown.




In this case, you could extract each point for the control group and the treatment group and calculate mean±SD across the continuous variable. But, if the continuous variable was a key moderator of interest in your analysis, it’d be lost from your meta-analysis.
Alternatively, you could calculate two Zr effect sizes, one for the ‘control group’ and one for the ‘treatment group’. The control group and moderator factor would then be a moderator—if this is how the rest of your dataset is designed.
As you can see, there might be no perfect solution. Care and thought are necessary to make this type of data comparable to other effect sizes in your dataset.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
section: Time series with a binary predictor
text:
Time series with a binary predictor
Sometimes the data is presented as a time series with a discrete intervention at one point in the time series, such as the introduction or eradication of a species. For example:







Figure 16— Simulated response over ten years (1995-2004). Blue points are before the intervention (1995-1999) and orange points are after it (2000-2004). The dashed line marks the intervention. No error bars are shown.




You’ll also encounter cases with only a few measurements on one side of the intervention:








The measurements before and after the intervention form one interrupted time series. Consecutive years are usually serially correlated, and the five years before the intervention are not naturally paired one-to-one with the five years after it. Treating the points as independent group replicates, or automatically using a paired SMD estimator ignores this non-independence.
In most cases, we expect you’ll exclude this data. However, if data is extremely limited you may want to take the mean±sd of the two groups (in this case “Present” and “Eradicated”) and calculate SMD or lnRoM. You could also calculate a correlation coefficient (Zr), treating the two groups as \(0\) or \(1\).
In either case, this requies calculating summary statistics off of non-independent samples. We therefore recommend, if you think this data is essential to include, to conduct sensitivity analyses including and excluding data summarized off of non-independent measurements. See our discussion of replication and non-independence here.






ImportantRecord the level of every summary



For every extracted mean and SD, record whether it summarizes measurements across individuals, space, time, or a combination of these. Also record the experimental or sampling unit that received the treatment. These fields make it possible to recognize incompatible units of replication or directions of summaries and to plan your sensitivity analyses.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Time series with error bars
What do you do if each of these measurements has associated error?








In this case, we recommend choosing the time point before and after the intervention and extracting the means and sd for an SMD or lnRoM effect size. Because the samples are paired, use a paired estimator of of your estimand.
Unfortunately, this ignores what may seem like an obvious and important pattern from the earlier and later measurements. However, sadly, the observational study design lack spatial controls, meaning that the pattern is lost to the sea of unusable data.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Geometric mean
Some studies report geometric means instead of arithmetic means. If the response is log-normally distributed and the reported dispersion is a geometric standard deviation, the geometric mean (\(m_{geo}\)) and geometric SD (\(sd_{geo}\)) can be converted to an arithmetic mean (\(m_a\)) and arithmetic SD (\(sd_a\)):
\[\begin{aligned}
&Var_{ln} = log(sd_{geo})^2 \\
&m_a = m_{geo} * e^{\frac{Var_{ln}}{2}} \\
&sd_a = m_a * \sqrt{e^{Var_{ln}} - 1} \\
\end{aligned}\]
In R:

sd_g <- 2.5
m_g <- 31

var_ln <- log(sd_g)^2
m_a <- m_g * exp(var_ln/2)
sd_a <- m_a * sqrt(exp(var_ln) - 1)

c("final_mean" = m_a, "final_sd" = sd_a)

final_mean   final_sd 
  47.17111   54.10126 


The arithmetic SD can be much larger than the geometric SD because a geometric SD is a multiplicative factor rather than a dispersion measured in the response’s original units.






Warning



Do not apply this conversion when the reported error is an arithmetic SD, SE, or confidence interval around a geometric mean.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
section: Means or standard deviations equal to 0
text:
Means or standard deviations equal to 0
A zero mean and a zero standard deviation create different problems. However this situation is possible with extreme results: every single island with an introduced predator (your predictor) has 0 prey (your response variable). In this case, the mean for the islands with introduced predators would be 0 with a standard deviation of 0.
SMD can include zero or negative means as long as at least one groups’ standard deviation is \(>0\). In this case, your data is almost certainly heteroscedastic and you should use the SMDH formulation of SMD (measure = "SMDH" in escalc), which has to be applied to all the data in your dataset. In ecological meta-analysis, we expect that SMDH is likely the preferred formulation because heteroscedasticity is common (and a subject interesting in its own right, see our discussion of variability effect sizes)






Warning



If both groups have an SD of 0, the usual SMD is undefined because there is no within-group variation with which to standardize the mean difference.


The lnRoM point estimate requires two positive means on a meaningful ratio scale. It is undefined when either mean is 0. Rather than adding the same arbitrary constant, such as 0.01, to every kind of response, you can define the smallest positive resolution for each outcome before calculating effect sizes. This is the smallest positive change that the biology, measurement method, and study design could have reported. It might represent one crossing, one animal, one colony, or the detection limit of an assay.
However, as we demonstrated here, lnRoM values can be gigantic if one of the means is near 0. Think carefully about whether lnRoM is the appropriate estimand for your question.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
Missing error bars
Many studies report means but do not report standard deviations (\(SDs\)), standard errors, or confidence intervals. Without them, we cannot calculate the sampling variance of an effect size, and the study is usually dropped. Dropping studies wastes data and can bias the overall result.
Nakagawa et al. (2023) showed that for lnRoM, we can replace missing standard deviations with the weighted average \(CV\) (\(CV = SD/m\)) from the studies that did report \(SDs\). This retains studies that would otherwise be excluded, provided the means are positive and lnRoM answers the biological question.
The sampling variance of lnRoM can be written in terms of each group’s \(CV\) and sample size:
\[
v_{\text{lnRoM}} = \frac{CV_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{CV_2^2}{n_2}
\]
\(SDs\) cannot be borrowed from other studies, because they depend on each study’s units and scale. \(CVs\) can be, because they have been standardized by the mean unitless. So when a study is missing its SDs, we can use an average \(CV\) from the studies that reported them.
Unfortunately, this only works for lnRoM. For standardized mean difference (SMD), the \(SD\) is part of the effect size itself, not only its sampling variance, so an average \(CV\) cannot stand in for it.
Before you impute

Check the article, supplementary material, and any data repository for the missing \(SD\).
Back-calculate \(SDs\) from other reported statistics: standard errors (\(SD = SE \times \sqrt{n}\)), confidence intervals, test statistics, or figures.
Contact the authors.
Decide how you will handle any remaining missing \(SDs\) before you look at the results, and write it in your protocol.
Two approaches
Nakagawa et al. (2023) describe two ways to use the average \(CV\):

Missing-cases approach: use observed study-specific SDs where available and an average CV to estimate sampling variances only for cases with missing SDs.
All-cases approach: use average-CV sampling variances for every effect size, creating a consistent weighting scheme across studies with and without reported SDs.

Neither approach should be selected because it gives a preferred result. Compare them with a complete-case analysis and report the proportion of effects with missing SDs, the CV estimator, and how the conclusion changes.
In metafor

escalc() has two average-\(CV\) options for measure = "ROM":


vtype = "AV": one average \(CV\) for group 1 and another for group 2, each weighted by sample size.

vtype = "AVHO": a single average \(CV\) pooled across both groups. Use this if you expect the two groups to have similar CVs.

On its own, vtype = "AV" applies the all-cases approach. To get the missing-cases approach, give vtype a vector: "LS" (the default, study-specific) for rows with SDs, and "AV" for rows without.






WarningSet correct = FALSE



Since metafor 4.8-0, escalc() applies a small-sample bias correction to lnRoM by default (Lajeunesse2015?) (see here). That correction uses the SDs, so yi is returned as NA for any row with a missing SD, even though vi is calculated. Set correct = FALSE when using vtype = "AV" or "AVHO" with missing SDs, or use the manual calculation below, which applies the bias correction with the average \(CV\) instead.


Worked example
We’ll use dat.curtis1998, a classic ecological lnRoM dataset on how elevated CO2 affects woody plant mass. It has complete SDs, so we’ll delete SDs from about 30% of the papers and compare each approach against the answer from the full data.
Let’s demonstrate. We’ll load a dataset included in metafor and set some standard deviations to NA and then use both the missing-cases and all-cases approach.

library(metafor)

dat <- dat.curtis1998

# Effect sizes from the full data, for reference
dat_full <- escalc(measure = "ROM",
                   m1i = m1i, sd1i = sd1i, n1i = n1i,
                   m2i = m2i, sd2i = sd2i, n2i = n2i,
                   data = dat, correct = FALSE)

# Delete both SDs for ~30% of papers. Missingness usually happens at
# the paper level, so we delete by paper rather than by row.
set.seed(2026)
papers <- unique(dat$paper)
miss_papers <- sample(papers, round(0.3 * length(papers)))

dat_miss <- dat
dat_miss$sd1i[dat_miss$paper %in% miss_papers] <- NA
dat_miss$sd2i[dat_miss$paper %in% miss_papers] <- NA

no_sd <- is.na(dat_miss$sd1i) | is.na(dat_miss$sd2i)
mean(no_sd)  # proportion of effect sizes with missing SDs

[1] 0.2058824


Now calculate the effect sizes three ways:

# 1. Complete-case: rows with missing SDs get vi = NA and are
#    dropped when the model is fitted
dat_cc <- escalc(measure = "ROM",
                 m1i = m1i, sd1i = sd1i, n1i = n1i,
                 m2i = m2i, sd2i = sd2i, n2i = n2i,
                 data = dat_miss, 
                 correct = FALSE) # Must specify uncorrected estimator

# 2. Missing-cases: study-specific variance where SDs exist,
#    average-CV variance where they don't
dat_mc <- escalc(measure = "ROM",
                 m1i = m1i, sd1i = sd1i, n1i = n1i,
                 m2i = m2i, sd2i = sd2i, n2i = n2i,
                 data = dat_miss, 
                 correct = FALSE,
                 vtype = ifelse(no_sd, "AV", "LS")) # Vector of `vtypes`

# 3. All-cases: average-CV variance for every row
dat_ac <- escalc(measure = "ROM",
                 m1i = m1i, sd1i = sd1i, n1i = n1i,
                 m2i = m2i, sd2i = sd2i, n2i = n2i,
                 data = dat_miss, 
                 correct = FALSE,
                 vtype = "AV")

Fit the same multilevel model to each, with effect sizes nested within papers.

fit <- function(d) rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | paper/id, data = d)

models <- list(
  "Full data (reference)" = fit(dat_full),
  "Complete-case"         = fit(dat_cc),
  "Missing-cases"         = fit(dat_mc),
  "All-cases"             = fit(dat_ac)
)

data.frame(
  k        = sapply(models, function(m) m$k),
  estimate = sapply(models, function(m) round(coef(m), 3)),
  ci.lb    = sapply(models, function(m) round(m$ci.lb, 3)),
  ci.ub    = sapply(models, function(m) round(m$ci.ub, 3))
)

                        k estimate ci.lb ci.ub
Full data (reference) 102    0.258 0.214 0.301
Complete-case          81    0.255 0.209 0.300
Missing-cases         102    0.261 0.218 0.304
All-cases             102    0.290 0.229 0.350


The complete-case analysis loses about a fifth of the effect sizes. Both average-\(CV\) approaches keep all of them.
Interestingly, the all-cases estimate differs from the full-data reference more than the others do. This is not caused by the missing data. In fact, running the all-cases approach on the complete dataset gives the same estimate as when we analyzed ‘dat_miss’.

# All-cases approach on the COMPLETE data (no SDs deleted)
dat_ac_full <- escalc(measure = "ROM",
                      m1i = m1i, sd1i = sd1i, n1i = n1i,
                      m2i = m2i, sd2i = sd2i, n2i = n2i,
                      data = dat, vtype = "AV", correct = FALSE)
coef(fit(dat_ac_full))

  intrcpt 
0.2895167 


The difference comes from the weighting. CVs in this dataset range from about 0.01 to 1.25, and sample sizes are small (median n = 5). Nakagawa et al. (2023) note that the all-cases approach can be biased in exactly this situation, when CVs differ strongly among studies and samples are small, and that the missing-cases approach may then be more reliable.
Here, the missing-cases estimate is closer to the full-data reference. To check how much CVs vary in your own data, run a meta-analysis of lnCVR and look at the between-study variance. When the two approaches disagree, report both.
Matching Nakagawa et al. (2023) exactly
vtype = "AV" differs from the paper’s all-cases method in three ways:

It uses the first-order variance formula shown above. Nakagawa et al. (2023) uses a second-order formula (Lajeunesse2015?).
With correct = FALSE, the point estimate is not bias-corrected. The paper bias-corrects it using the average CVs.
It averages CVs across all effect sizes at once, weighted by sample size. The paper first averages CVs within each study, then averages those across studies, weighted by each study’s mean sample size. This stops studies that contribute many effect sizes from dominating the average CV.

To follow the paper exactly, calculate the effect sizes by hand:

# Step 1: within each study, average the CVs (weighted by sample size)
#         and the sample sizes. Studies with missing SDs are left out.
obs <- subset(dat_miss, !is.na(sd1i) & !is.na(sd2i))
by_study <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(obs, obs$paper), function(s) data.frame(
  cv1 = weighted.mean(s$sd1i / s$m1i, s$n1i),
  cv2 = weighted.mean(s$sd2i / s$m2i, s$n2i),
  n1  = mean(s$n1i),
  n2  = mean(s$n2i))))

# Step 2: average across studies, weighted by each study's mean sample size
cv1 <- weighted.mean(by_study$cv1, by_study$n1)
cv2 <- weighted.mean(by_study$cv2, by_study$n2)

# Step 3: bias-corrected point estimate and second-order sampling variance
dat_ac2 <- dat_miss
dat_ac2$yi <- with(dat_ac2, log(m1i / m2i) + 0.5 * (cv1^2 / n1i - cv2^2 / n2i))
dat_ac2$vi <- with(dat_ac2, cv1^2 / n1i + cv2^2 / n2i +
                            cv1^4 / (2 * n1i^2) + cv2^4 / (2 * n2i^2))

fit(dat_ac2)


Multivariate Meta-Analysis Model (k = 102; method: REML)

Variance Components:

            estim    sqrt  nlvls  fixed    factor 
sigma^2.1  0.0112  0.1058     29     no     paper 
sigma^2.2  0.0144  0.1199    102     no  paper/id 

Test for Heterogeneity:
Q(df = 101) = 208.2638, p-val < .0001

Model Results:

estimate      se    zval    pval   ci.lb   ci.ub      
  0.2886  0.0310  9.3128  <.0001  0.2279  0.3494  *** 

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


In this example the result (0.289) is almost identical to vtype = "AV" (0.290), even though papers contribute between 1 and 18 effect sizes each. For most datasets, vtype = "AV" with correct = FALSE is a reasonable shortcut.






Note



Note that for sensitivity analyses, you should consider (at least) three analysis sets:

Using only the studies that reported standard deviation (and using the yi and vi returned by escalc)
Using the yi and vi returned by escalc alongside the “missing cases” calculations of yi and vi (type = "AV")
Using the yi and vi from the “all-cases” method (calculated manually, as above)









Important



If your data is overdispersed, then an alternative is to calculate the inverse of effective sample size (\(1/N_0\)), and use this as your model weight. See above and Nakagawa et al. (2023). Note that doing so limits you to lnRoM, since SMD requires \(sd\) in the point estimator formula and thus requires \(sd\) directly.
Effective sample size is defined as: \[
\begin{aligned}
&N_{0} = \frac{4n_1n_2}{n_1 + n_2}\\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
From the t statistic
Calculating SMD from test statistics depends on whether the data come from a paired design (in which case df = n-1) or an independent two-sample design (df = n_1 + n_2 - 2). This is the formula for calculating SMD from a unpaired, two-sample design t test statistic:
\[\begin{aligned}
&d=t*\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}} \\
&J= 1 - \frac{3}{4(n_1 + n_2 - 2) - 1} \\
&g=J*d \\
&Var(g) = \frac{n_1 + n_2}{n_1 n_2} + \frac{g^2}{2(n_1 + n_2 - 2)} \\
\end{aligned}\]
In escalc you simply specify the t statistic (with ti), as well as sample sizes for each group (n1, n2) and use measure “SMD”, which will return the unpaired SMD estimate.

t = -1.5
n1 = 15
n2 = 15

escalc(measure = "SMD",
       ti = t,
       n1i = n1,
       n2i = n2)


       yi     vi 
1 -0.5329 0.1381 


For a paired design, the paired \(t\) statistic gives you a standardized mean change: the mean difference divided by the SD of the differences, \(d_z = t/\sqrt{n}\). That isn’t on the same scale as an ordinary SMD. To put it on the SMD (raw-score) scale, multiply by \(\sqrt{2(1-\rho)}\). This assumes equal pre and post SDs and needs a pre-post correlation \(\rho\) (use 0.5, with 0.8 as a sensitivity analysis):
\[\begin{aligned}
&d_z=\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}} \\
&d=d_z\sqrt{2(1-\rho)} \\
\end{aligned}\]
escalc applies the small-sample correction and returns the variance for the paired estimate, so you do not need to compute \(J\) or \(Var(g)\) by hand.
Then hand that \(d\) to escalc with measure = "SMCRP". The trick is to enter \(d\) as the treatment mean, 0 as the control mean, and 1 for both SDs, so the standardized difference escalc calculates is just \(d\). Supply the assumed correlation and the number of pairs. We show the change-score version, SMCC, for comparison:

t = -1.5
n_pairs = 15
rho = 0.5

d_z <- t / sqrt(n_pairs)
d_raw <- d_z * sqrt(2 * (1 - rho))

escalc(measure = "SMCRP",
       m1i = d_raw, m2i = 0,
       sd1i = 1, sd2i = 1,
       ri = rho,
       ni = n_pairs)


       yi     vi 
1 -0.3742 0.0696 


The raw-score version (SMCRP) is on the same metric as an independent-groups SMD, so it can be pooled with other SMDs.






Note



An alternative estimand, the change-score version (SMCC) divides by the SD of the change scores. It estimates a different quantity and should not be pooled with independent-groups SMDs. This can be calculated in a similar fashion:

escalc(measure = "SMCC",
       ti = t,
       ni = n_pairs)


       yi     vi 
1 -0.3661 0.0711

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
From p values:
When only a two-sided \(p\) value from an independent two-group \(t\) test is reported, escalc uses the unusual convention that the sign attached to the input \(p\) value supplies the missing effect direction. Confirm the direction from the reported means, figure, or text before using this route.

p = -0.07
n1 = 15
n2 = 15

escalc(measure = "SMD",
       pi = p,
       n1i = n1,
       n2i = n2)


       yi     vi 
1 -0.6693 0.1408

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
From F statistic
For a test with one numerator degree of freedom, \(|t|=\sqrt{F}\). The \(F\) statistic does not contain the direction of the contrast, so the sign must come from reported means, a coefficient, a figure, or clear text. An omnibus \(F\) test with more than two groups or more than one numerator degree of freedom does not identify one two-group SMD by itself.
Needs clarification. How to calculate.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
section: Least Square Means (LS Means) or Estimated Marginal Means
text:
Least Square Means (LS Means) or Estimated Marginal Means
Estimated marginal means are adjusted model predictions. They are not interchangeable with raw arithmetic means, and their SEs are not within-group SDs.
Sadly, this data is lost to the seas of unusable data.

title: Continuous outcomes between two groups
text:
PCAs — risky business
Imagine you are conducting a meta-analysis of risk-taking in animals. You are including a variety of behavioral responses: flight initiation distances, vigilance, activity rate, and so on. All of these are considered proxies for risk-taking (and you are of course looking at these both combined and separately because you are a sensitivity-analysis master).
Then you come upon a real stumper of a study. They used a principal components analysis (PCA) to synthesize the exact same variables you are interested in into a single ordination space. The first axis of this ordination space (PC1) has synthesized all the variables you are interested in into a single variable. This might look like this:







Figure 17— Simulated PC1 and PC2 scores for five treatment and five control sites (n = 5 per group), with arrows showing the loadings of three behaviors. PC1 is the axis of interest. No error bars are shown.




The authors also provide this (though you could extract it from the points in the figure above as well):








Is this data usable?
Before extracting these means±sd, we recommend looking for raw data or contacting the authors. If these prove to be fruitless, and your dataset is small and hungry, it might be worth using the PC1 scores. However, be certain that the PC axis is synthesizing variables that are otherwise considered legitimate responses in your dataset.
And be careful: you should conduct sensitivity analyses excluding this data to ensure that your results are robust.
Next: Discrete outcomes between two groups: lnOR and lnRR

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
Many effect sizes can be inter-converted (Borenstein et al. 2021, Lajeunesse 2026) These conversions make assumptions and can bias the resulting effect types (see (Poom and Wåhlberg 2022)) and should be carefully used—with sensitivity analyses to ensure that the conversions aren’t unduly influencing results.
At the same time, especially for questions with limited data, we believe that conversions are an important tool in the meta-analyst toolkit.


Effect size types


Converting effect sizes requires several assumptions. We summarize these in the table below:






Conversion
Assumption



lnOR ↔︎ SMD
Response variable is a discretized version of an underlying continuous variable


SMD ↔︎ Zr
Predictor variable is a discretized version of an underlying continuous variable


lnOR ↔︎ Zr
Response and predictor have an underlying continuous reality


SMD ↔︎ lnRoM
Homogeneity of variances between groups



In addition to these assumptions, be careful that the data is truly comparable, especially in terms of their units of replication—otherwise the converted effect size will have vastly higher or lower weights in the final meta-analytic model.
For example, imagine you’re analyzing the effect of an introduced predator on prey abundance. Some studies present abundance correlations of the predator and prey (Zr), where the unit of replication is the number of surveys. Other studies report the presence and absence of prey species on islands with and without the predator (lnOR), for which the unit of replication is number of islands (each of which was presumably surveyed many times).
Both of these study types are relevant to the same question–—the effect of the predator on prey abundance. Likewise, converting betwee these effect sizes does not violate the assumptions in the table above because presence-absence is a discretized version of abundance. It is thus possible to convert these effect sizes via SMD to include both papers in the same model.
However, the units of replication of these study types are vastly different (study 1 = survey; study 2 = island). This means the Zr abundance correlations will have more weight than the full-island lnOR responses.
However, in many other cases, conversions will allow similar data to be compared without comparing different units of replication.
Given the assumptions and potential biases involved in converting effect sizes, we recommend that you convert minority effect sizes to the dominant effect size in your dataset after confirming that assumptions are met and that the unit of replication for all the effect sizes are equivalent. We then recommend running your models with and without these converted effect sizes, to evaluate whether the inclusion of minority effect sizes alter your results.






ImportantAlternative to conversion: reconstruct the underlying data



In some cases, converting between effect sizes can be prevented by reconstructing the underlying data of the author-presented summaries and summarizing these data into the desired analysis effect size, which can align the units of replication between studies.
See examples for SMD-type effect sizes, lnOR effect sizes, Zr effect sizes, and for non-Gaussian responses



We have digitized the primary conversion formulas and they are available in our convert_effect_sizes() function. Running the function on its own will return a table with the statistics required for each conversion.

convert_effect_sizes()


Effect type name must be specified with 'effect_type' argument
    and provide necessary variables (as named arguments, e.g., n1 = group1_n or a numeric vector).
 
Returning effect size names & required variables for reference.


   from_effect to_effect  vars_required
        <char>    <char>         <char>
1:        lnOR       SMD yi, vi, n1, n2
2:          Zr       SMD      yi, vi, n
3:           r       SMD           r, n
4:         SMD        Zr yi, vi, n1, n2
5:         SMD      lnOR yi, vi, n1, n2
6:       lnRoM       SMD yi, vi, n1, n2
7:          Zr      lnOR      yi, vi, n
8:        lnOR        Zr     yi, n1, n2


To convert an effect size, specify the from effect type and the to effect type, as well as the required statistics. Note that this function also supports full, two-step conversions from Zr to lnOR and vice versa.
We’ll now show the math and demonstrate the conversions in R. SMD is the universal solvent of these conversions and it is important to remember that SMD has multiple estimators. The most commonly used is Hedges’ \(g\), which has a small sample size bias correction factor \(J\). However, all conversion formulas convert to and from \(d\), an alternative estimator of SMD that lacks this correction factor. For that reason, the math below will skip this conversion and be written for \(d\) instead of \(g\) based on this conversion.
\[
\begin{aligned}
&J = 1-\frac{3}{4*(n_1 + n_2 - 2) - 1}\\
&d = \frac{m1-m2}{sd_{pooled}}\\
&d = \frac{g}{J}
\end{aligned}
\] Note that the default sampling variance estimator for Hedges’ g is the same estimator used for Cohen’s d (in the R package escalc. Thus no conversion from Var(d) to Var(g) is necessary.






ImportantAlternative estimators and effect size conversion



As described earlier in this tutorial, there are multiple flavors of estimators for many effect sizes including paired estimators and, for SMD, an estimator that tolerates heteroscedastic data (“SMDH”). To the best of our knowledge, there are no conversion formulas for these alterative estimators.
This means that if you are converting Zr effect sizes to add to a meta-analysis that is otherwise composed of SMD-type effect sizes, you won’t be able to use SMDH for the larger dataset. Conversely, if you have paired SMD-type data that you wish to convert to add to a meta-analysis of Zr effect sizes, you’ll have to ignore the paired design.

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
SMD → lnOR
This conversion assumes that the response variable is continuous (e.g., undergirding the binary response of the lnOR effect type) and that it has a logistic distribution (similar to a normal distribution).
If the lnOR data was presence/absence of a species and the SMD data was abundance, we believe this assumption is satisfied, given that presence/absence are the extreme ends of abundance.
Let \(yi_{lnOR}\) and \(yi_{d}\) be the point estimate for the lnOR and Cohen’s d effect sizes and \(vi_{lnOR}\) and \(vi_{d}\) be their sampling variances:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_{lnOR} = yi_d * \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}} \\
&vi_{lnOR} = vi_{d} * \frac{\pi^2}{3} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

convert_effect_sizes(from = "SMD",
                     to = "lnOR",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes that the continuous data has a logistic distribution. 
Please use conversions carefully and conduct sensitivity analyses. 
Note that the 'vi' is assumed to have been calculated with `metafor::escalc` package defaults (variance of 'd' not 'g') 


   yi_trans   vi_trans
      <num>      <num>
1: 1.677835 0.03289868

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
SMD → Zr
This conversion assumes that a continuous variable was discretized to form the treatment and control groups of an SMD effect size. This may be the case in some situations (e.g., if treatment and control were based on the presence or absence of an independent variable treatment while the correlation was across a continuous gradient of the same variable).
To convert from SMD to Zr, we first convert \(d\) to the correlation coefficient \(r\) and then to Zr, using a correction factor \(a\) for cases where \(n_1 \neq n_2\). Let \(yi_{Zr}\) and \(yi_d\) be the point estimate for Zr and Cohen’s d:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&a = \frac{(n_1 + n_2)^2}{n_1*n_2} \\
&r = \frac{yi_d}{\sqrt{yi_d^2 + a}} \\
&r \leftarrow \min(1, \max(-1, r_i))\\
&yi_{Zr} = atanh(r)\\
\end{aligned}
\]
And the sampling variance of Zr (\(vi_{Zr}\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
&n = n1 + n2 \\
&vi_{Zr} = \frac{1}{(n - 3)} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

convert_effect_sizes(from = "SMD",
                     to = "Zr",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes a continuous variable was dichotomized to create the treatment and control groups. 
Note that the 'vi' is assumed to have been calculated with 'metafor::escalc' defaults (variance of 'd' not 'g'). 
Like usual, be careful :) 


    yi_trans   vi_trans
       <num>      <num>
1: 0.4474395 0.03703704








Important



Instead of converting SMD to Zr, it may be preferable to calculate a biserial correlation coefficient directly from the same summary statistics used for SMD, and convert this (\(r_b\)) to Zr. This can be done in escalc directly with the measure “ZBIS”, which calculates teh biserial correlation coefficient and converts it to Zr.

escalc(measure = "ZBIS",
       m1i = 10, m2i = 7,
       sd1i = 1.5, sd2i = 2,
       n1i = 15, n2i = 15)


      yi     vi 
1 1.1788 0.1135 


Note that there is also an option to calculate a point-biserial correlation coefficient (\(r_{pb}\)) from naturally discrete groups (e.g., male versus female). However, Jacobs and Viechtbauer (2017) advised against comparing this to correlation coefficients calculated from 2 continuous variables (\(r\)) or from one artificially discretized variable (\(r_b\)).
Confusing stuff…My head hurts.

title: Converting between effect sizes
text:
Zr → SMD
First, convert the point estimate of Zr (\(yi_{Zr}\)) to the correlation coefficient \(r\) and calculate the variance of \(r\) (\(vi_r\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
&r = tanh(yi_{Zr}) \\
&vi_r = \frac{(1-r^2)^2}{(n-1)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Then calculate the point estimate (\(yi_d\)) and variance (\(vi_d\)) of Cohen’s d:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_d = \frac{2*r}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \\
&vi_d = \frac{4*vi_r}{(1-r^2)^3} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

convert_effect_sizes(from = "Zr",
                     to = "SMD",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Multiple events per individual
lnOR and lnRR describe discrete events. Each individual (or plot) can only experience one event. You can only die once.
Howevever, you may be interested in events that can occur multiple times to the same individual. For instance, the number of infections or the number of times a plot burns or the number of times an individual breeds.
Event counts, also known as person-time data, require a different effect sizes. The three main estimands are the log incidence rate ratio, incidence rate difference, and square-root transformed incidence rate difference.
These effect sizes are supported in escalc with measure options of “IRR”, “IRD”, and “IRSD” respectively. All of these effect sizes require x1i, x2i (which describe the number of events) and t1i and t2i which is total ‘person’ times (number of persons or plots * time monitored). Note that you need to standardize the total time monitored before calculating.
These effect sizes are not commonly used in ecology and evolution, so we will discuss these much more. However, data like this should not be analyzed with lnOR or lnRR like other binary outcomes.

title: Continuous predictors: assumptions and interpretation
text:
As you have seen so far in this guide, effect sizes are not trivial things. Together, point estimates and sampling variances are small statistical models with their own numerical assumptions, properties, and quirks. Understanding these assumptions is essential if you want to conduct a proper and robust meta-analysis, and if you want to correctly interpret these effect sizes and the outputs of meta-analytic models.
In this section, we discuss effect sizes for describing the relationship strength between two continuous variables. These are known as measures of association. While the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient (\(r\)) is the most intuitive and widely reported metric in primary studies, its mathematical properties make it problematic for direct meta-analytic pooling. Instead, we will dive into the elegant statistical world of Fisher’s Z-transformed correlation coefficient (\(Z_r\)), our variance-stabilizing alternative.






NoteEffect sizes for slope of a relationship, not association



As we discuss further below, \(Z_r\) describes the strength of an association between two variables in terms of both direction and consistency of relationship (e.g., scatter).
However, sometimes you’re not interested in the strength of an association between two variables but just the slope—for instance when looking at rate of change of a response through time.
For these types of questions, you can use the slopes from linear models. We discuss this in the appendix, here.



Why can’t we just pool raw correlations?
When primary studies report their results, they often present Pearson’s correlation coefficient (\(r\)). It is an appealing effect size: it carries no units, so a correlation between body mass and clutch size can be compared directly against one between soil nitrogen and plant diversity (if that makes sense to be compared, which is another question). It runs from \(-1\) (a perfect negative linear association) through \(0\) (no linear association) to \(+1\) (a perfect positive linear association).
In practice, many studies never report \(r\) at all. Instead, they show a scatterplot, often with a fitted line from a linear model, and report a slope, a \(t\) or \(F\) statistic, or an \(R^2\). In those cases you will have to obtain \(r\) yourself, either by extracting the points from the figure (see Chapter 3.4) or by converting the reported test statistics (see Chapter 4).






TipWhat \(r\) actually measures



It is easy to forget, if your last stats class was a while ago, that \(r\) packs two things into a single number: the direction of the relationship and how tightly the points cluster around a straight line. It is not the slope. The two are linked by
\[
r = b \, \frac{s_x}{s_y}
\tag{1}\]
where \(b\) is the slope of the regression of \(y\) on \(x\), and \(s_x\) and \(s_y\) are the standard deviations of the two variables. The same slope can therefore come with a strong or a weak correlation, depending on how much scatter surrounds the line, and a very shallow slope can give \(r\) close to \(1\) if the points sit right on it (Fig. 1). Squaring \(r\) gives \(r^2\), the proportion of the variance in \(y\) explained by a straight line on \(x\) (the same \(R^2\) as in a simple linear regression).

Codeset.seed(42)
n <- 50
x <- rnorm(n)
e <- as.numeric(scale(resid(lm(rnorm(n) ~ x))))  # noise uncorrelated with x, so the fitted slope equals b exactly
scenarios <- data.frame(
  panel = c("A. Steep slope, little scatter", "B. Steep slope, lots of scatter", "C. Shallow slope, little scatter"),
  b     = c(1, 1, 0.2),
  sigma = c(0.4, 2, 0.08)
)
sim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(scenarios)), function(i) {
  data.frame(panel = scenarios$panel[i], x = x,
             y = scenarios$b[i] * x + scenarios$sigma[i] * e)
}))
labs_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(sim, sim$panel), function(d) {
  data.frame(panel = d$panel[1],
             label = sprintf("slope = %.2f\nr = %.2f", coef(lm(y ~ x, data = d))[2], cor(d$x, d$y)))
}))
p <- ggplot(sim, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "dodgerblue3", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = labs_df, aes(x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = label),
            hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1.2, size = 3.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Predictor (x)", y = "Response (y)")
p






Figure 1— Three simulated datasets with the same 50 values of \(x\). Panels A and B share the same slope but differ in scatter, so their correlations differ. Panels A and C have very different slopes but the same scatter relative to the slope, so their correlations are identical.




For a meta-analysis, this means that two studies of identical biology (same slope) can report different correlations simply because one measured noisier data or sampled a narrower range of \(x\) (see range restriction and measurement error below).


Convenient as it is, the raw correlation coefficient has three mathematical properties that sit awkwardly with the assumptions of standard meta-analytic models. All three trace back to a single issue: \(r\) is bounded by \(-1\) and \(+1\), and statistical estimates behave badly near hard limits.

The estimate gets squeezed against the ceiling. When the true correlation in the population is near zero, repeated studies scatter symmetrically around it. When the true correlation is strong, say \(+0.8\), there is simply less room to overshoot than to undershoot, because no estimate can exceed \(+1\). The spread of plausible estimates becomes lopsided, with a long tail on the low side. The practical cost is that confidence intervals calculated the usual way assume a symmetric spread, so they end up miscalibrated and can even extend beyond \(1\), which does not make sense. Separately, and through a different route, \(r\) is a slightly shrunken estimate of the true correlation. It is pulled toward zero, whatever its sign. That shrinkage is small (for a true correlation of \(0.5\) measured on \(20\) individuals, roughly \(0.01\)), but it is the reason unbiased alternatives to \(r\) exist (Olkin and Pratt 1958).
Precision is tangled up with the result. Meta-analysis weights each study by its precision, and this only works if precision is governed by something independent of the answer, such as sample size. For correlations it is not. The sampling variance of \(r\) is:

\[
v_i = \frac{(1 - r_i^2)^2}{n_i - 1}
\tag{2}\]

As such, variance contains the correlation itself. The larger the magnitude of the correlation a study happens to report (or the closer \(|r_i|\) is to \(1\)), the smaller its variance and the heavier its weight. A study that overestimated the magnitude of the correlation by chance is therefore rewarded with extra influence, and the pooled estimate is dragged away from zero. Notice that this pushes in the opposite direction to the shrinkage in point 1, above. The same entanglement distorts funnel plots and inflates the false-positive rate of Egger’s test for funnel asymmetry. The scatter narrows toward correlations with large magnitudes for reasons that have nothing to do with genuine precision.



Small samples make matters worse. Meta-analytic models assume each study’s estimate is drawn from a bell-shaped distribution around the true value. For correlations, that approximation holds up well with large samples and modest effects, and it breaks down when the sample is small and the correlation is strong—the combination most familiar to anyone working with a dozen populations or a handful of species.

To solve these issues, Fisher proposed a variance-stabilizing, normalizing transformation (Fisher 1921, Borenstein et al. 2021).
The statistical mechanics of \(Z_r\)

1. Fisher’s \(Z\) transformation (the point estimate)
Fisher’s transformation stretches the bounded \([-1, +1]\) interval across the entire number line, pushing the ceilings out to infinity so that estimates are no longer squeezed against them. Formally, it is the inverse hyperbolic tangent (\(\text{atanh}\)):
\[
y_i = Z_{r_i} = \text{atanh}(r_i) = \frac{1}{2} \ln\left(\frac{1 + r_i}{1 - r_i}\right)
\tag{3}\]
Both equal signs are exact: \(\frac{1}{2} \ln\left(\frac{1 + r}{1 - r}\right)\) is simply the definition of \(\text{atanh}(r)\). The approximations come in later, when we describe how \(Z_r\) is distributed across studies.
Correlations near zero barely move. Correlations near the boundaries are stretched dramatically. The result is a distribution that is close to symmetric and close to normal for samples of roughly \(10\) or more.
2. The sampling variance
The real beauty of Fisher’s transformation lies in its sampling variance. After transformation, the sampling variance depends on sample size and nothing else:
\[v_i = \text{Var}(Z_{r_i}) = \frac{1}{n_i - 3} \tag{4}\]
The effect size has vanished from the variance entirely. Studies are now weighted purely by how much data they collected, which is exactly the assumption meta-analytic models were built on. Symmetry and approximate normality come along for free.






NoteThe variance formula assumes bivariate normality



Fisher’s variance is derived assuming the two variables follow a bivariate normal distribution. This requires not only that each variable is marginally normal, but that their joint distribution is bivariate normal (implying a linear relationship, elliptical contours of equal probability density, and homoscedastic residual variance across the range of the predictor). See here to explore this distribution.
When the underlying data are strongly non-normal (heavy tailed) abundance counts, or ratios with a few extreme values, the true sampling variance can be noticeably larger than \(1/(n_i - 3)\), and standard errors will be too optimistic (Kowalski 1972, Hawkins 1989). This is a further reason to prefer robust variance estimation (see below) when your evidence base is built on skewed ecological data.
What about a discrete variable, such as a binary treatment, a sex, or a presence/absence response? Pearson’s formula will still return a number (the point-biserial correlation), but a binary variable cannot be normal, so the bivariate normality assumption fails by construction. The variance \(1/(n_i - 3)\) becomes a rough approximation, and the correlation itself is capped by how unevenly the two groups are split (see the point-biserial box under Not all correlations are comparable). For these designs, an SMD or \(\ln\text{OR}\) is usually the better effect size. Discrete variables with many ordered levels (for example, counts spanning a wide range) are less of a problem, but the same caution applies.


3. Back-transformation to \(r\)

We conduct all statistical modeling, random-effects estimation, and moderator tests in the \(Z_r\) metric, but \(Z_r\) values are difficult to interpret conceptually. An effect size of \(Z_r = 1.1\) means very little to our brain until we convert it back to \(r = 0.8\). We therefore back-transform final pooled estimates from our meta-analytic models, and the confidence intervals, to the more intuitive correlation scale using the hyperbolic tangent (\(\tanh\)):
\[r = \tanh(Z_r) = \frac{e^{2 Z_r} - 1}{e^{2 Z_r} + 1} \tag{5}\]
In R, this looks like:

tanh(1.1)

[1] 0.800499








WarningBack-transformation is not a neutral operation



Because the conversion from \(Z_r\) to \(r\) is curved rather than straight, back-transforming a pooled estimate does not return the arithmetic mean of the underlying correlations. Under the standard random-effects assumption that true effects are normally distributed on the \(Z_r\) scale, it returns the exact median of the distribution of true correlations on the \(r\) scale. Furthermore, by Jensen’s inequality (since \(\tanh\) is strictly concave for positive values), this median exceeds the arithmetic mean of the underlying correlations in magnitude, and the gap between median and mean widens as between-study heterogeneity grows. In ecology and evolution, where heterogeneity is usually substantial, a back-transformed estimate will typically have a larger magnitude than the true average correlation across studies.
Three practical consequences:

Interval bounds back-transform safely. Because the transformation preserves rank order, converting the two ends of a confidence or prediction interval gives valid bounds on the \(r\) scale. So, convert the endpoints, never the standard error.
Heterogeneity does not back-transform at all. Report \(\tau^2\), \(I^2\), and prediction intervals on the \(Z_r\) scale, or convert the prediction interval endpoints only. There is no meaningful “\(\tau^2\) in correlation units.”
Word your conclusion carefully. “The pooled effect corresponds to a correlation of 0.42” is defensible; “the average correlation across studies was 0.42” is not, once heterogeneity is appreciable.

Some authors (notably the Hunter–Schmidt tradition; Hunter and Schmidt (2014); Field (2001)) respond to this by pooling raw correlations with sample-size weights instead. We use Fisher’s \(Z_r\) throughout this guide because it solves three problems at once, but the choice is genuinely contested and worth considering.


Code and formula pairing: implementation in R
Let’s look at how to implement these calculations in R using metafor::escalc and basic math. Note that in many cases, the \(Z_r\) effect sizes that you calculate in a meta-analysis will involve multiple steps. Few studies report \(r\) directly. Instead many of those studies will present scatterplot visualizations, which they analyze with linear models. To calculate \(r\) (the precursor to \(Z_r\)), you’ll have to extract the points from the scatterplot (or find their raw data) and calculate \(r\) across the points.
As such, your raw dataset will be long, with a row per measurement point and an ID to specify the summarization group to calculate \(r\). The sample size (\(n_i\)) for each study will be the number of data points extracted for that specific study.
Once \(r\) and \(n\) are calculated the operation is simple. We’ll here show both calculating manually and with escalc.

# Simple demonstration of Zr transformation and back-transformation in R

# Let's say we have extracted a correlation of r = 0.6 from a study of n = 50
r_val <- 0.6
n_val <- 50

# 1. Manual Fisher's Z transformation
z_manual <- 0.5 * log((1 + r_val) / (1 - r_val))
var_manual <- 1 / (n_val - 3)

# 2. Using escalc from metafor
dat_example <- data.frame(ri = r_val, ni = n_val)
dat_zr <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR", ri = ri, ni = ni, data = dat_example)

print(paste("Manual Z:", round(z_manual, 4)))

[1] "Manual Z: 0.6931"

print(paste("escalc Z (yi):", round(dat_zr$yi[1], 4)))

[1] "escalc Z (yi): 0.6931"

print(paste("escalc Z (vi):", round(dat_zr$vi[1], 4)))

[1] "escalc Z (vi): 0.0213"

# 3. Back-transformation using tanh
r_back <- tanh(z_manual)
print(paste("Back-transformed r:", round(r_back, 4)))

[1] "Back-transformed r: 0.6"








NoteFisher’s \(Z\) in metafor



The metafor package (Viechtbauer 2010) implements Fisher’s \(Z\) transformation via the measure code "ZCOR". This is the measure you want for the workflow in this chapter.
You may also encounter "UCOR", which applies the Olkin-Pratt correction (Olkin and Pratt 1958) for the small-sample shrinkage described above. Be aware that "UCOR" returns a corrected raw correlation, not a transformed one. So it fixes the shrinkage while leaving the variance-effect entanglement fully intact. It is not an upgraded version of "ZCOR", and the two should not be mixed within a single analysis. In general, we know of few cases where "UCOR" should be used instead of "ZCOR".


Let’s plot how \(r\) maps to \(Z_r\). Notice how the relationship is nearly a straight line around zero but curves sharply as it approaches the boundaries of \(-1\) and \(+1\):

r_seq <- seq(-0.99, 0.99, by = 0.01)
zr_seq <- atanh(r_seq)

plot_data <- data.frame(r = r_seq, zr = zr_seq)

ggplot(plot_data
  , aes(x = r
      ,y = zr)
  ) +
  geom_line(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  labs(title = "Fisher's r-to-Z transformation"
    , x = "Raw correlation (r)"
    , y = "Fisher's Z (Zr)") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray")













TipWhat happens when \(r = \pm 1\)?



Follow the curve above to its ends: as \(r\) approaches \(\pm 1\), \(Z_r\) heads off to \(\pm\infty\). At exactly \(r = \pm 1\), Fisher’s transformation is undefined, since \(\text{atanh}(1) = \infty\). The variance, however, looks perfectly well behaved, because \(1/(n_i - 3)\) ignores \(r\) entirely. Nothing in the variance formula warns you that something has gone wrong.
escalc deals with this by recoding the infinite values to NA (with a warning). metafors modeling function, rma.mv will drop those rows before model fitting (with another warning). The consequence is easy to miss: the studies reporting the strongest associations quietly disappear from your analysis, pulling the pooled estimate toward zero.

# Three studies; study A reports a perfect correlation

                          , ri = c(1, 0.45, 0.30)
                          , ni = c(8, 40, 60))

dat_perfect <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR", ri = ri, ni = ni, data = dat_perfect)
