A reported \(r = \pm 1\) almost always points to one of the following:


A tiny sample. Any two points lie on a straight line, so \(r = \pm 1\) is guaranteed at \(n = 2\) and common at \(n = 3\) or \(4\). At \(n \le 3\) the variance is undefined anyway, and escalc returns NA for \(v_i\).

Rounding. A table reporting \(r = 1.00\) may hide an \(r = 0.996\).

Aggregated data. Correlations among a handful of group means are inflated toward \(\pm 1\) (see ecological correlations below).

Variables that are not independent. One variable is computed from the other (e.g., body mass vs. a mass-based condition index), or the same measurement was entered twice.
Extraction or reporting errors.

What to do:


Go back to the source and work out which of these applies. Fix errors, and exclude correlations between variables that were not measured independently.

If rounding is the likely cause, replace the value with the largest correlation consistent with the reported precision (e.g., \(0.995\) for a reported \(1.00\)), and flag it.

Never pick an arbitrary ceiling without checking its influence. Because \(Z_r\) explodes near the boundary, the choice matters a great deal:


ceilings <- c(0.99, 0.995, 0.999, 0.9999)

# Fisher's Z for each candidate ceiling
round(atanh(ceilings), 2)

[1] 2.65 2.99 3.80 4.95

# Pooled estimate (back-transformed to r) when study A's r = 1 is replaced by each ceiling
sapply(ceilings, function(r_max) {
  dat_ceiling <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR"
                        , ri = pmin(ri, r_max)
                        , ni = ni
                        , data = dat_perfect)
  round(tanh(unname(coef(rma(yi, vi, data = dat_ceiling)))), 3)
})

[1] 0.798 0.838 0.904 0.955


Without study A, the pooled correlation is \(r = 0.36\). Put study A back in, and the pooled correlation lands anywhere between \(0.80\) and \(0.96\), depending only on which ceiling you picked. A single tiny study with \(n = 8\) ends up dominating the synthesis. Its inflated \(Z_r\) makes the between-study variance balloon, and that flattens the weights of the larger studies.
Run your models with and without these studies, and under more than one ceiling. Report how much the pooled estimate depends on them.


Interpretation and benchmarks: what does \(r\) mean?
When interpreting your pooled \(Z_r\) effect size, you may encounter the traditional benchmarks proposed by Jacob Cohen (1988):








Effect size class
Correlation coefficient (\(r\))
Variance explained (\(r^2\))
Interpretation



Small
\(0.1\)
\(1\%\)
Subtle effect, barely visible to the naked eye.


Medium
\(0.3\)
\(9\%\)
Visible to a careful observer; typical of many social and ecological processes.


Large
\(0.5\)
\(25\%\)
Prominent relationship; easily detectable.



These labels were offered by Cohen as a fallback for researchers with no domain knowledge to draw on, and he said so explicitly. The interpretation of effect sizes is highly context-dependent:

In evolutionary ecology, natural selection operates on tiny margins. A correlation of \(r = 0.05\)—explaining a quarter of one percent of the variance—can be strongly adaptive and shape survival over generations (Kingsolver et al. 2001, Nakagawa and Santos 2012).
In biomedical research, regular aspirin consumption has an effect on heart attack risk equivalent to \(r = 0.034\). This explains about one tenth of one percent of the variance, yet translates to thousands of lives saved annually (Rosenthal 1990).

Never apply Cohen’s benchmarks blindly. Always interpret your pooled correlations in the context of the biology, the decision costs, and the practical implications of the phenomenon.
Not all correlations are comparable
Before converting anything, check that the correlations you have extracted are estimating the same quantity. Several common mismatches will quietly corrupt an otherwise careful meta-analysis.
Partial correlations are not zero-order correlations. A study reporting the association between temperature and growth rate after controlling for body size is reporting a different parameter from a study reporting the raw association. Pooling the two together answers no clear question. If you must include partial correlations, flag them, model them as a moderator, and adjust the sample size to account for the covariates that were controlled for (the variance is closer to \(1/(n_i - k_i - 3)\), where \(k_i\) is the number of control variables; Fisher (1924); Aloe and Thompson (2013)).
Range restriction shrinks correlations (Thorndike 1949, Sackett and Yang 2000). A study sampling across a narrow elevational band will report a weaker correlation than one spanning the full gradient, even if the underlying biology is identical. Where you can, record range or standard deviation of the predictor and use it as a moderator.
Measurement error shrinks correlations too (Spearman 1904, Hunter and Schmidt 2014). Noise proxies attenuate associations toward zero. If reliability estimates are available for some studies and not others, this becomes a source of heterogeneity you cannot see.






TipEcological (aggregate) correlations vs. individual correlations



Ecological correlations are not individual correlations. When primary studies report correlations among group means (such as site averages) rather than individual measurements, they are estimating an ecological correlation (Robinson 1950). Because group averaging washes away individual-level residual variance, aggregate correlations are almost always substantially stronger (larger \(|r|\)) than individual-level correlations (aggregation bias / Robinson’s paradox).
Mixing ecological correlations with individual correlations in the same meta-analysis introduces severe methodological heterogeneity. When the individual is the intended unit of replication across the synthesis, researchers sometimes reconstruct individual-level distributions from group means and standard deviations (see Chapter 3.4, Section 3.4.3).
However, this is an experimental simulation technique: all reconstructed individuals share identical group-level predictor values, creating cluster-level pseudoreplication that requires multilevel models or robust variance adjustments to avoid artificially deflating standard errors.








TipContinuous predictors with binary outcomes (Point-biserial & Biserial)



Point-biserial and Biserial correlations. When a continuous predictor is paired with a truly discrete binary outcome (e.g., predator density vs. nest fledged/failed), calculating Pearson’s formula yields the point-biserial correlation (\(r_{pb}\)). A key mathematical constraint of \(r_{pb}\) is that when paired with a continuous normal variable, \(|r_{pb}|\) can never mathematically reach 1.0: its theoretical maximum is capped at \(\sqrt{2/\pi} \approx 0.798\) even under a perfectly balanced 50/50 split (\(p = q = 0.5\)), and shrinks further when base rates are uneven (Jacobs and Viechtbauer 2017).
In contrast, the biserial correlation (\(r_b\)) assumes the binary outcome reflects an underlying continuous trait with a threshold, correcting for this attenuation. Fortunately, point-biserial correlations can also be converted to Standardized Mean Differences (\(d\)) or log Odds Ratios (\(\ln\text{OR}\)) to unify continuous and discrete studies within the same synthesis (see Chapter 3.4, Section 3.4.5 and Chapter 4).


Handling ranked correlations: Spearman’s \(\rho\) and Kendall’s \(\tau\)

When voyaging through the literature, you will inevitably encounter studies that present raw data, scatterplots, or matrices, that need to be analyzed as \(Z_r\) but are based on ranks rather than raw values. Or you will encounter studies that do not report Pearson’s \(r\). Instead, because their data were non-normal or ranked, they reported Spearman’s rank correlation (\(\rho\) or \(r_s\)) or Kendall’s tau (\(\tau\)).

Spearman’s \(\rho\) is Pearson’s \(r\) computed on the ranks of each variable rather than on their raw values. It measures how well the relationship is described by any monotonic curve, not just a straight line.
Kendall’s \(\tau\) looks at every pair of observations and asks whether they are ordered the same way on both variables (a concordant pair) or in opposite ways (a discordant pair): \(\tau = (C - D) / \binom{n}{2}\), where \(C\) and \(D\) are the numbers of concordant and discordant pairs. It is less sensitive to outliers and ties than \(\rho\), and usually smaller in magnitude for the same data.

In R, both are available through cor(x, y, method = "spearman") and cor(x, y, method = "kendall").
Because these metrics are based on ranks rather than raw values, their numeric scales are slightly compressed compared to Pearson’s \(r\). To include these studies in your meta-analysis, you can apply the following transformations to approximate their Pearson equivalents:
Spearman’s \(\rho\) to Pearson’s \(r\):
\[r \approx 2 \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6} \rho\right) \tag{6}\]
Kendall’s \(\tau\) to Pearson’s \(r\):
\[r \approx \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} \tau\right) \tag{7}\]
Both formulas assume the underlying data are bivariate normal (Kendall 1948, Rupinski and Dunlap 1996), which is very often the assumption the original authors doubted when they chose a rank method in the first place. Treat the conversions as approximations.
A useful refinement: once converted and Fisher-transformed, an effect size originating from Spearman’s \(\rho\) is slightly noisier than one originating from Pearson’s \(r\). Because ranks discard some metric information, converted rank correlations have slightly lower statistical efficiency than Pearson correlations, inflating the sampling variance of \(Z_r\) by about 6% under bivariate normality (Fieller et al. 1957, Myers and Sirois 2004):
\[v_i \approx \frac{1.06}{n_i - 3} \tag{8}\]
As such, these converted effect sizes will have slightly less influence on your meta-analytic models, which is a conservative adjustment. For Kendall’s \(\tau\), the converted correlation has an asymptotic relative efficiency of \(9/\pi^2 \approx 0.912\) under bivariate normality, implying a variance inflation factor of \(\approx \pi^2/9 \approx 1.10\). While some practitioners apply \(v_i \approx 1.10 / (n_i - 3)\), many retain \(1/(n_i - 3)\) as a working approximation and evaluate its impact through sensitivity analysis (comparing models with and without converted correlations).






TipConverting rank correlations in R



Here is the full workflow for a small dataset mixing Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall correlations: convert to Pearson equivalents, flag the conversions, compute \(Z_r\), and inflate the variance of the Spearman-derived effect sizes.

# Conversions to Pearson-equivalent r (@eq-spearman and @eq-kendall)
spearman_to_r <- function(rho) 2 * sin(pi / 6 * rho)
kendall_to_r  <- function(tau) sin(pi / 2 * tau)

dat_ranked <- data.frame(study = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F")
                         , type = c("pearson", "pearson", "pearson"
                                    , "spearman", "spearman", "kendall")
                         , reported = c(0.42, 0.31, 0.55, 0.38, 0.60, 0.25)
                         , ni = c(35, 60, 22, 50, 42, 28))

dat_ranked$ri <- ifelse(dat_ranked$type == "spearman", spearman_to_r(dat_ranked$reported),
                 ifelse(dat_ranked$type == "kendall", kendall_to_r(dat_ranked$reported),
                        dat_ranked$reported))

# Flag converted effect sizes for sensitivity analyses
dat_ranked$is_converted <- dat_ranked$type != "pearson"

dat_ranked <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR", ri = ri, ni = ni, data = dat_ranked)

# Inflate the sampling variance of Spearman-derived effect sizes (@eq-rank-inflation)
dat_ranked$vi <- ifelse(dat_ranked$type == "spearman", dat_ranked$vi * 1.06, dat_ranked$vi)

ImportantSensitivity analyses as best practice



Never treat these conversions as magic solutions. Approximations introduce uncertainty. Always flag converted effect sizes in your dataset (e.g., is_converted = TRUE) and run sensitivity analyses. Specifically, run your meta-analytic models both with and without the converted Spearman and Kendall correlations. If your overall effect size or its uncertainty shifts substantially, you must report this and be cautious in your interpretations.


The “unit of replication” obsession
A central theme of our guide is the unit of replication. When calculating and meta-analyzing measures of association, ensuring that the unit of replication aligns across studies is paramount. Mismatches in the level of replication will alter your sample size, your sampling variance, and consequently how much influence each study has on your pooled result.
Consider a study examining the correlation between soil nitrogen and plant diversity:


Study A measures the correlation across 50 individual quadrats (\(n = 50\)).

Study B measures the correlation across 5 distinct geographic sites, where each site represents the pooled average of 10 quadrats (\(n = 5\)).

Even if both studies report an identical correlation of \(r = 0.5\), Study A carries roughly 47 units of weight against Study B’s 2. A difference of more than twentyfold (!), driven entirely by a decision about what counts as a replicate. If site is the true independent unit of replication, treating Study A’s quadrats as independent replicates is pseudoreplication (Hurlbert 1984).






NoteWeights are not simply \(n - 3\)



The figures above assume a common-effects model, where a study’s weight is one over its sampling variance. In the random-effects and multilevel models you will actually fit, weight is one over the sampling variance plus the between-study variance \(\tau^2\). That extra term acts as a floor on everyone’s uncertainty and compresses the differences between studies considerably: with a moderate \(\tau^2\) of \(0.1\), the twentyfold gap above shrinks to roughly fivefold. Large studies still dominate, but far less absolutely than the raw sample sizes suggest.


Before running your models:

Identify the true, independent unit of replication for each study.
Standardize or aggregate correlations where necessary to avoid inflating sample sizes.
When in doubt, perform sensitivity analysis by adjusting sample sizes to reflect conservative biological units of replication.
When primary studies report only group-level summaries (mean \(\pm\) SD error bars) and individual-level replication is required, you can simulate individual-level distributions to align replication units (see Chapter 3.4, Section 3.4.3 for worked protocols), being mindful that this induces clustered data.

Non-independence, matrices, and tagging
Correlation coefficients frequently violate the assumption of independence. Several traps exist in continuous predictor meta-analyses:
1. Pairwise correlation matrices (the melting trap)
Primary studies somtimes present a correlation matrix comparing multiple traits or environmental factors. Meta-analysts sometimes “melt” these matrices and include all pairwise correlations as separate effect sizes.
For example, imagine a single study measures body mass, wing length, and tarsus length on the same sample of 40 birds and reports a \(3 \times 3\) correlation matrix. Melting this matrix yields three pairwise correlations (mass–wing, mass–tarsus, wing–tarsus) from the exact same individuals. Treating these three estimates as independent data points inflates your sample size and produces artificially narrow standard errors.






WarningMelted matrices cause non-independence that grows quadratically



If a study measures 5 traits on a single set of individuals, it generates \(\frac{5 \times (5-1)}{2} = 10\) pairwise correlations. Those 10 correlations share the exact same subjects. Treating them as independent data points inflates your Type I error rate, because the model behaves as though you had ten times more information than you actually collected.


To handle this non-independence:

Use multilevel meta-analysis with a random effect for study or paper identity to absorb shared variance (Noble et al. 2017).
Where the same individuals contribute to several correlations, construct an explicit variance-covariance matrix with metafor::rcalc rather than relying on random effects alone.
Combine either approach with robust variance estimation (Hedges et al. 2010, Pustejovsky and Tipton 2018) (metafor::robust, or the clubSandwich package) so that your standard errors remain trustworthy even if the assumed covariance structure is imperfect.







TipMixing studies that need rcalc with studies that do not



The variance-covariance matrix (\(\mathbf{V}\)) covers the whole dataset, but it is block-diagonal: effect sizes from different studies have zero covariance, so each study contributes its own block. A study with a single correlation contributes a \(1 \times 1\) block, which is simply its \(v_i\). rcalc builds these blocks for you: pass it all studies at once, and the ones reporting a single correlation end up with their usual variance on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. With rtoz = TRUE, it works directly on the \(Z_r\) scale.

# Study A reports a 3 x 3 correlation matrix for the same 40 birds;
# studies B, C, and D each report a single correlation
dat_mix <- data.frame(
  study = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "C", "D"),

  var2  = c("wing", "tarsus", "tarsus", "growth", "growth", "growth"),
  ri    = c(0.50, 0.40, 0.60, 0.30, 0.25, 0.45),
  ni    = c(40, 40, 40, 25, 60, 33)
)

When the correlations between effect sizes are unknown, metafor::vcalc builds the same block-diagonal structure from an assumed within-study correlation (e.g., rho = 0.6). 2. Dyadic and interaction matrices
Another common form of matrix data in ecology and animal behavior is the dyadic interaction matrix (e.g., grooming frequencies vs. agonistic support across all pairs in a group, or genetic vs. geographic distance; Schino (2007)).
In an \(N \times N\) matrix of \(N\) individuals, there are \(N(N-1)/2\) dyadic pairs. Melting this matrix into pairwise rows creates non-independence because each individual appears in \(N-1\) separate dyads (as both actor and recipient). The true independent unit of replication is the number of individuals or social groups (\(N\)), not the number of dyadic pairs (\(N(N-1)/2\)). Treating dyads as independent observations inflates sample sizes quadratically and produces falsely narrow confidence intervals. (For practical extraction and matrix handling, see Chapter 3.4, Section 3.4.6).
3. Temporal autocorrelation and effective sample size
When correlating two continuous variables measured repeatedly over time (e.g., annual population density vs. annual temperature anomalies), sequential observations typically exhibit serial autocorrelation.
Autocorrelation violates the assumption of independent errors, drastically reducing the effective sample size (\(n_{\text{eff}} < n\); Pyper and Peterman (1998)). If the nominal number of time points \(n\) is plugged directly into \(v_i = 1/(n-3)\), the sampling variance will be heavily underestimated, causing the time series to dominate the pooled meta-analysis with spuriously high weight. Always flag time-series correlations in your metadata and consider adjusting sample size for serial autocorrelation (see Chapter 3.4, Section 3.4.4).
4. Spatial and temporal flagging
Continuous predictors in ecology and evolution often vary across spatial and temporal grains. Always record and flag metadata for:


Spatial grain: e.g., local plot size, regional \(\text{km}^2\).

Temporal grain: e.g., seasonal correlation, decadal trend.

Flag groupings: flag studies sharing common study sites, common control subjects, or common experimental treatments.

Figure 2— Decision steps for turning a reported association into a Fisher’s Z effect size. Chapter 3.4 covers the extraction steps, and Chapter 4 covers conversions from other effect sizes.






To ensure your meta-analysis is rigorous, stick to the following workflow:


Extract raw data: Record the correlation, its sample size, the type of correlation reported, whether it is zero-order or partial, and the unit of replication (see Chapter 3.4 for extracting from scatterplots, error bars, time series, and matrices).

Screen for comparability: Set aside or flag partial correlations, and note any study with obvious range restriction or unreliable measurement.

Standardize conversions: Convert any Spearman’s \(\rho\) or Kendall’s \(\tau\) to Pearson’s \(r\) equivalents (see Chapter 3.4, Section 3.4.1). Flag these.

Reconstruct grouped data where necessary: If studies report group means \(\pm\) SD error bars and individual-level replication is required, simulate individual-level distributions to align replication units, accounting for clustered pseudoreplication (see Chapter 3.4, Section 3.4.3).

Calculate Fisher’s \(Z_r\): Transform raw and converted correlations using metafor::escalc(measure = "ZCOR").

Address non-independence: Check for multi-trait matrices, dyadic interactions, and shared subjects (see Chapter 3.4, Section 3.4.6). Nest non-independent effect sizes within study using multilevel random effects and construct V-matrices where appropriate.

Run models: Fit multilevel random-effects models in the \(Z_r\) metric, paired with robust variance estimation.

Test sensitivity: Re-run models excluding converted metrics, small-sample outliers, or pseudoreplicated studies.

Back-transform for reporting: Convert pooled estimates and interval endpoints back to \(r\) using tanh. Keep heterogeneity statistics on the \(Z_r\) scale, and word your conclusions to reflect what the back-transformed value actually represents.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
TEST
\(Z_r\) describes correlations between a continuous predictor variable and a (generally) continuous response variable. \(Z_r\) is thus an important effect size in the meta-analyst tool kit, especially with observational data.
\(Z_r\) type data often takes the form of a scatterplot but other formats exist (e.g., matrices, time series, and model estimates). We’ll go through these examples in turn, along with solutions and limitations for extracting \(Z_r\) type data. We’ll start, however, by describing how to structure a database for \(Z_r\) type effect sizes.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
Database design
In general, \(Z_r\) effect size extractions require a long-format database for data entry, where each row is one of the points in the corresponding analysis. This is because you will most likely be extracting individual points from scatterplot figures, instead of directly reported correlation coefficients (\(r\)).
This dataset will then be summarized in R to derive \(r\) (using cor.test) and sample size (\(n\)), producing a derived dataset with a single row per unique correlation. Be sure to have clear ID columns to help with summarization. Alternatively, you can calculate \(r\) and \(n\) while extracting data but this may lead to clunkiness in your workflow.
Note that some studies (though rarely in our experience) will report the raw correlation coefficients (\(r\)) and sample size (\(n\)), which will require a simpler data entry format (1 row per correlation coefficient). These can be entered into the same raw dataset or into a separate tab.






ImportantTypes of directly reported correlations



The \(Z_r\) effect size is based on a transformation of Pearson’s correlation coefficient (\(r\)). However, there are other correlation types. Spearman correlation is used for non-parametric correlation tests, Kendall for XXXXX, biserial for an artificially discretized predictor variable, and point-biserial for a truly discretized predictor variable.
Of these, it appears that all but point-biserial can be used to calculate \(Z_r\) without adjustment (Jacobs and Viechtbauer 2017). escalc has measure arguments directly designed to convert biserial correlations to \(Z_r\) (measure = "ZBIS").


Your dataset may look like this, with the first correlation (corr_1) represented as raw data extracted from a scatterplot and the second correlation (corr_2) entered directly as the correlation coefficient and sample size:

This will then be summarized in R to calculate the correlation coefficient \(r\) and sample size. We offer a helper function get_r that allows you to do this more succinctly:

get_r <- function(x, y){
  out <- cor.test(x, y)
  return(out$estimate)
}

# Summarize the raw correlation data:
dat.summarized <- dat %>%
  filter(!is.na(x)) %>%
  group_by(correlation_id) %>%
  summarize(r = get_r(x, y),
            n = n())

# Bind with the already summarized correlation data:
dat.final <- rbind(dat.summarized,
                   dat %>% 
                     filter(!is.na(r)) %>%
                     select(-x, -y))

# Now calculate Zr:
dat.summarized <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR",
                         ri = r, ni = n,
                         data = dat.final)

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
Simple figures
This is the simplest type of correlation figure. In this case, you’d calibrate the x and y axes and extract each point. Then use cor.test in R to calculate the correlation coefficient:







Figure 1— Simulated scatter of 50 points (grey) with a least-squares line. Each point is one observation, so n = 50. There are no error bars.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
Overplotting
But what if there is an ugly cluster of overlapping points?







Figure 2— Simulated scatter of 50 points (grey). The pink points are 11 copies of one point (row 5) jittered to show an overplotted cluster of 12 observations at one location. There are no error bars.




If the total number of points is reported for the study, you can duplicate the values of the pink points as many times as it takes to match the total sample size. Otherwise, you’ll just have to digitize as many as you can and use a sample size that may be less than the real sample size (which makes the overall \(Z_r\) estimate more conservative—e.g., less weight in the model).
In the figure above, we could safely eyeball 5 separate points (though in reality there are 12).

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
Single axis error bars
But what do you do if each point is actually a mean±SD?







Figure 3— Mean y ± SD for each site (grey points, error bars show ±1 SD), with a least-squares line through the site means. Each point is one site; the internal sample size per site is 10 measurements.




Let’s imagine that each point is a site. Most researchers likely ignore the \(SD\) and calculate \(Z_r\) from the site means and number of sites, as follows:

head(dat)

          x         y        sd     n
      <num>     <num>     <num> <num>
1: 6.835348  6.777621 0.4643857    10
2: 6.006148  7.009790 0.3391786    10
3: 7.263167  9.731899 0.2513182    10
4: 7.598918 10.632717 0.4530599    10
5: 7.145446  8.584171 0.4681221    10
6: 5.063659  5.643530 0.3626755    10

out_site <- cor.test(dat$x, dat$y)
site_mean_estimates <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR",
                               ri = out_site$estimate,
                               ni = nrow(dat))
site_mean_estimates


      yi     vi 
1 1.1225 0.0213 


However, calculating \(Z_r\) this way treats site as the unit of replication. If the other studies in your dataset also treat site as the unit of replication, this is the best approach. However, if the rest of your data uses individuals or plots as the unit of replication you will end up with misaligned units of replication.
An alternative approach is to simulate the underlying data behind each site-level summary (i.e., the points in the scatterplot above). This can help align the units of replication with your dataset and ensure that studies with higher effort have more influence in your models. To do so:

Determine the internal sample size of each point, i.e., how many measurements were summarized to produce the means ± error.
Extract the means and error and convert error to \(SD\)
Use these statistics to draw random samples of of the data underlying each point from the appropriate statistical distribution (with the length of this sample equal to the internal sample size).

Note that this process can align the unit of replication of this data with the rest of your dataset. However, it also introduces a different issue: the individual observations are not equally independent (i.e., they’re clustered within each point). Luckily, there is a way to correct for this, which we’ll demonstrate below.
Here we’ll use rnorm to draw normally distributed data for each point. Note that it is also possible to draw data from other distributions (see here and here for a worked example with a \(Z_r\)-type effect size and the binomial distribution)






Warning



Note that reconstructing underlying data is an experimental method. Use carefully.


The first few rows of our extracted data looks like this, with an internal sample size of 10 measurements per site:

In a loop, we draw data for each site:

y_expanded <- list()

for(i in 1:nrow(dat)){
  y_expanded[[i]] <- data.table(y = rnorm(mean = dat$y[i],
                                          sd = dat$sd[i],
                                          n = dat$n[i]),
                                x = dat$x[i])
}
y_expanded <- rbindlist(y_expanded)

nrow(y_expanded)

Warning



If the author-provided data presents standard error (or confidence intervals, etc) instead of standard deviation, remember that you absolutely must convert these to standard deviation before attempting to reconstruct the underlying distribution. See here on how to convert from other measures of error to standard deviation.


If you were to plot this reconstructed data, it would look like this:








In this example, each point had an internal sample size of 10 measurements. The reconstructed dataset therefore has 500 rows (50 sites times 10 measurements), but these rows are not fully independent. All measurements within a site share the site’s x value and the associated spatial or temporal clustering.
So how do we deal with the non-independence among these simulated observations?
We shrink the sample size with a design effect (see here) by calculating the intraclass correlation (ICC). This describes the amount of variation between sites rather than within sites. We estimate it from the scatter of the site means around the regression line and from the within-site SDs:

out <- cor.test(y_expanded$x, y_expanded$y)

fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = dat)
s2_w <- mean(dat$sd^2)                                    # within-site variance
s2_b <- max(var(resid(fit)) - s2_w / mean(dat$n), 0)      # between-site variance
icc <- s2_b / (s2_b + s2_w)
n_eff <- nrow(y_expanded) / (1 + (mean(dat$n) - 1) * icc) # effective n

n_eff

[1] 57.31979


The effective sample size became 57—much closer to the number of sites (50) than the total number of observations (500). If the standard deviations around each point had been larger, then effective sample size would be larger and further approach the number of individual measurements.
To calculate \(Z_r\), we calculate \(r\) from the expanded x and y variables:

# Now calculate 'r':
out <- cor.test(y_expanded$x, y_expanded$y)
r <- out$estimate
r

      cor 
0.7886448 


But instead of using 500 as our sample size in our call to escalc, we use our estimate of effective sample size:

escalc(measure = "ZCOR",
       ri = out$estimate,
       ni = n_eff)


      yi     vi 
1 1.0678 0.0184 


Compare this to our site-level \(Z_r\) estimates (n=50), that ignored the error bars:

site_mean_estimates


      yi     vi 
1 1.1225 0.0213 


You can see that sampling variance decreased and the point estimate shifted. You’ll also notice that in this example, the overall influence of simulating the underlying data had only minor influence on our estimates. Take that as you will. Regardless we think this is pretty neat.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
section: x and y axis error bars
text:
x and y axis error bars
What do you do if there are also error bars on the x axis? For example, if each point is a mean±SD of two different measurements. This is common in field studies, where researchers may sample vegetation at a site and some other factor (e.g., animal activity or soil nutrients) and then present the means±SD of each site in a correlation.







Figure 4— Mean y (vertical error bars, ±SD) against mean x (horizontal error bars, ±SD) for all 50 sites. Each point is one site, so the correlation below is an ecological (aggregate) correlation with n = 50 sites.




In this case, the safest bet is likely to use the data as is, tagging the unit of replication as being site-level instead of measurement-level.
However, it is possible to simulate the data underlying these bivariate distributions (bivariate in that they concern correlated x and y measurements). This is, as above, an experimental data reconstruction technique. Use this only if your data is limited and you think it’s essential to glean as much data as possible.

Click here to see a full demonstration
In the table below, you’ll see the extracted mean values for the x and y variables (x, y), their standard deviations (x_sd, y_sd), and their internal sample sizes (x_n and y_n), which differ. To draw from a bivariate distribution we need to use a single sample size. To be conservative, we’ll use whichever sample size is smallest. We’ll then use mvrnorm in the R package MASS.

library("MASS")

head(dat)

          x         y      y_sd   y_n       x_sd   x_n
      <num>     <num>     <num> <num>      <num> <num>
1: 6.835348  6.777621 0.4643857    10 0.13655035    20
2: 6.006148  7.009790 0.3391786    10 0.05417928    20
3: 7.263167  9.731899 0.2513182    10 0.41916233    20
4: 7.598918 10.632717 0.4530599    10 0.24139897    20
5: 7.145446  8.584171 0.4681221    10 0.09851552    20
6: 5.063659  5.643530 0.3626755    10 0.15615917    20

# Choose the n with the lowest sample size:
dat[, n := min(c(x_n, y_n))]

# Specify `rho`, the correlation between x and y:
r <- 0.5

xy_expanded <- list()

for(i in 1:nrow(dat)){
  # Create the correlation matrix between x and y:
  sig <- matrix(
                c(dat$x_sd[i]^2,
                  r * dat$x_sd[i] * dat$y_sd[i],
                  r * dat$x_sd[i] * dat$y_sd[i],
                  dat$y_sd[i]^2),
                nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE
              )
  
  # Draw from the multivariate normal distribution
  xy_expanded[[i]] <- mvrnorm(n = dat$n[i], 
                              mu = c(x = dat$x[i], 
                                     y = dat$y[i]), 
                              Sigma = sig) |>
    as.data.frame()
}
xy_expanded <- rbindlist(xy_expanded)

Our dataset went from 50 rows (one per point in the figure above) to 500 rows, given an internal N of 10 per point.
One issue with this approach is that, in ecology at least, it’s unlikely that the two bivariate distributions are the same. One might be a Beta distribution and the other negative binomial, etc. The normal distribution is unlikely to be the true data generating process (as assumed above).
However, if you do take this approach, the next step would be to calculate ICC and effective sample size (as above). And, as always, conduct sensitivity analyses!

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
Mismatched time series
However, what do you do if the time series are mismatched?
Below, we’ll plot two time series, one for Variable 1 and one for Variable 2:







Figure 6— Two mismatched time series. Variable 1 is sampled yearly (left panel) and Variable 2 is sampled every quarter year (right panel). These are simulated values to show the alignment problem.




What is the best way to line up variable 1 and variable 2 to calculate their correlation? While imputing the missing values in the second panel is one possible approach, it is the least conservative.
Instead, we recommend taking the average of the most frequently sampled variable to align with the less frequently sampled variable. Alternatively, you can filter the data (after aligning by the shared x-axis) to just those occassions where there is data for both series.
Aligning the data like this is tricky and will probably require manual merging based on nearest value in a spreadsheet software (e.g., Excel) after calibrating both the x and y axes.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
section: Discrete responses with a continuous predictor
text:
Discrete responses with a continuous predictor
Imagine you are conducting a meta-analysis concerned with factors driving nest success or failure in a seabird. Many of the studies use a discrete predictor, e.g., presence or absence of a predator. These types of data are naturally suited for lnOR or lnRR effect sizes.
However, other studies report mortality in relationship to the abundance of that predator—e.g., the continuous manifestation of presence/absence.







Figure 7— Simulated nest outcome (1 = fledged, 0 = failed) against predator abundance, one point per nest. The probability of fledging declines with abundance. Points are jittered vertically; n is given in the text.




Depending on your meta-analysis question you may want to extract this data and calculate a \(Z_r\) correlation effect size, which can then be converted to lnOR (see here) and compared to your other lnOR discrete-predictor effect sizes. To do so, extract each point, which is an individual, and calculate \(Z_r\) with the responses as a binary variable of 0 or 1.
This conversion is safe because presence/absence is a discretized version of abundance and because the unit of replication is the number of nests (or individuals) in both cases and the conversion formulas assume that discrete variables are discretized or extreme ends of a continuous variable (which is true with presence and absence).
Regardless, care is still necessary. It’s unclear the extent to which calculating \(Z_r\) on binary outcomes can estimate the estimand of lnOR. A potentially safer option is to extract the raw data and fit a logistic regression of nest fate on predator abundance. The coefficient is the lnOR per unit of abundance. However, it’s unclear whether this can be compared to other lnOR’s in your dataset. This was an idea from Santi but I’m not sure it’s comparable.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
section: Proportion data with a continuous predictor
text:
Proportion data with a continuous predictor
You can imagine similar challenges where instead of 0 or 1 responses, the authors report % of a population:







Figure 8— Proportion alive (y axis, a population-level summary) against temperature (degrees C), at nine temperature treatments. The proportion declines monotonically; there are no error bars.




You can calculate \(Z_r\) directly between the predictor (temperature, x-axis) and the proportion alive (the y axis), directly.
However, each location on the x-axis actually represents a population of individuals, all of whom were monitored to determine the proportion alive. As such, simply calculating \(Z_r\) directly from the proportion ignores population size and treats the number of surveys (or sites) as the unit of replication (n=10).
This can lead to a serious mismatch with the rest of your dataset—if the rest of your dataset is based the number of individuals as the unit of replication (like above)
To deal with this, the best option would be to convert the proportion data to binary response data based on the total number of individuals in each x-axis treatment—if this can be reconstructed from author reported summaries.
For example, if this figure reflects an experiment where each temperature treatment had 15 individuals, then you can multiply the survivorship at each temperature level by 15, and then expand this dataset to have a 0 or 1 for all 15 individuals per temperature treatment. Because each count is deterministic (rounded from the proportion), there is no added random noise.
Let’s give it a try. dt is a data.table with a column for proportion alive and for temperature. We’ll calculate the number of living and dead individuals, make the dataset long so that these are in one column, and then duplicate the dataset to be one row per individual. Finally, we’ll create a binary column of 0s and 1s:

dt[, number_alive := floor(proportion_alive * 15)]
dt[, number_dead := 15 - number_alive]
head(dt)

   temperature proportion_alive number_alive number_dead
         <num>            <num>        <num>       <num>
1:        10.0        0.8175745           12           3
2:        12.5        0.7057850           10           5
3:        15.0        0.5621765            8           7
4:        17.5        0.4073334            6           9
5:        20.0        0.2689414            4          11
6:        22.5        0.1645165            2          13

# Now melt dataset:
dt.mlt <- melt(dt, 
               measure.vars = c("number_alive", "number_dead"),
               variable.name = "status", 
               value.name = "n_individuals")
head(dt.mlt)

   temperature proportion_alive       status n_individuals
         <num>            <num>       <fctr>         <num>
1:        10.0        0.8175745 number_alive            12
2:        12.5        0.7057850 number_alive            10
3:        15.0        0.5621765 number_alive             8

title: Continuous predictors
section: Mean±SD proportion data with continuous predictor
text:
Mean±SD proportion data with continuous predictor
Now let’s look at a similar situation, except the figure is presenting mean±SD mortality across separate trials within each temperature treatment.








If we want our unit of replication to be based on the number of individuals, we need to try to reconstruct the underlying distributions behind each of these summarized trials. This will allow us to calculate a correlation across individuals for the binary response of being alive or dead, instead of across the mean per trial.
We also, of course need to figure out, from the text, the number of individuals and the number of trials (or sites, plots, etc) that the mean±sd were calculated from.






Note



A similar data structure could occur with discrete outcomes per plot instead of individuals with the number of sites/islands interchangeable with the number of trials.
An example would be the number of plots occupied by a species (the discrete outcome) per study site (the trial), which are sampled across some continuous gradient of interest.


To do this, we will do something similar as in the previous section. However we will use either the binomial or beta-binomial distribution instead of the normal distribution.

Click here for a full demonstration
To understand whether to use the binomial or beta-binomial distribution, we will check whether the observed (author-reported) standard deviation is greater than the theoretical standard deviation of the binomial distribution, which is defined by the proportion and the the number of individuals per trial.

theoretical_sd <- sqrt((dt$proportion_alive * (1 - dt$proportion_alive))/(dt$n_individuals))

nrow(dt[sd > theoretical_sd])

[1] 0


It looks like the reported standard deviations are all less than or equal to the theoretical standard deviation of the binomial family. So we can use the binomial distribution to generate the raw underyling data. See here for the equations and a fuller description, as well as how to generate data for beta-binomial distributed data (when \(sd_{reported} > sd_{theoretical}\)).
Now we’ll draw binomial data with the rbinom function. We specify size as number of individuals per trial (n_individuals in our dataset dt), n as number of trials (n_trials in our dataset), and p as the author reported mean proportion alive (proportion_alive). The function will return a numeric vector, with each element indicating the number of alive individuals per trial. With 3 trials, each vector should have a length of 3.






Warning



Note that reconstructing underlying data is an experimental method. Use carefully.


For a single temperature treatment, this looks like this:

rbinom(p = dt$proportion_alive[1],
       size = dt$n_individuals[1],
       n = dt$n_trials[1])

[1] 15 15 12


Each element of the vector reports the estimated number of individuals that survived of the 20 individuals in that trial.






Note



Note that if the number of individuals differed across trials within the same temperature treatment, you can provide a vector of values instead of a single value to the size argument:

rbinom(p = dt$proportion_alive[1],
       size = c(10, 15, 5),
       n = dt$n_trials[1])

[1]  7 11  4


However, in this case, we question whether the article’s authors should have summarized this data by mean±sd in the first place.


Now we’ll use a for loop to iterate over our dataset per temperature treatment. We’ll take the sum of the vector returned by rbbinom, which gives the total number of living individuals across the three trials.

y_expanded <- list()

for(i in 1:nrow(dt)){
  y_expanded[[i]] <- data.table(n_alive = sum(rbinom(p = dt$proportion_alive[i],
                                                     size = dt$n_individuals[i],
                                                     n = dt$n_trials[i])),
                                temperature = dt$temperature[i])
}
y_expanded <- rbindlist(y_expanded)

y_expanded[, n_dead := as.integer(n_dead)]

As with the section above, you can then expand this dataset from a row per temperature treatment to become a row per individual and temperature treatment, with a binary outcome variable of living or dead:

y_expanded.mlt <- melt(y_expanded, 
                       measure.vars = c("n_alive", "n_dead"),
                       variable.name = "status",
                       value.name = "n_individuals")

# Now expand to n rows per outcome:
final_dat <- y_expanded.mlt[rep(seq_len(.N), n_individuals), ]

# add a binary outcome:

If we had simply calculated Zr from the author-reported means, our sample size would have been 5 and our unit of replication would have been number of trials, instead of number of individuals.
Reconstructing the underlying binomial distribution as we did here gives the resulting effect size considerably higher weight in your meta-analytic models, and may help align your unit of replication to lnOR type effect sizes (if those are also in your dataset and you are planning on converting effect sizes).

res <- cor.test(final_dat$living, final_dat$temperature)

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
Matrices
Some types of correlations are more complicated because they are based on pairwise matrices that describe relationships between individuals. As such, each value is not independent because the same individuals engaged with other individuals.
For instance, correlations between pair-wise behaviors. An example would be the relationship between grooming behavior and defense, which was meta-analyzed by Schino (2007). Is grooming adaptive because it leads to mutual defense with grooming partners?
With data like this, you might have a directed matrix of grooming between individuals, and a second matrix of defense between the same individuals. Here we simulate 10 individuals, with defense correlated with grooming:

n_ind <- 10
groom <- matrix(runif(n_ind^2, min = 1, max = 100), nrow = n_ind)
diag(groom) <- NA

defend <- groom + matrix(rnorm(n_ind^2, mean = 0, sd = 15), nrow = n_ind)
diag(defend) <- NA

knitr::kable(round(groom[1:4, 1:4], 1))



NA

90.8

15.8

NA




Each off-diagonal cell is a directed dyad. Because the grooming matrix is directed, we use both triangles, so every off-diagonal value enters the calculation. We melt the two matrices into vectors of aligned dyads:

keep <- !is.na(groom)
dyads <- data.table(grooming = groom[keep], defence = defend[keep])
nrow(dyads)

[1] 90


Now calculate Kendall’s correlation across the dyads and convert it to a Pearson-equivalent r with \(r = \sin(\pi\tau/2)\) before calculating Zr. The sample size is the number of individuals, not the number of dyads:

tau <- cor(dyads$grooming, dyads$defence, method = "kendall")
r_matrix <- sin(pi * tau / 2)

escalc(measure = "ZCOR",
       ri = r_matrix,
       ni = n_ind)


      yi     vi 
1 1.5162 0.1429 


The dyads share individuals, so they are not independent, and the standard error above is only a first approximation. If the paper reports a Mantel or QAP test (permutation tests built for matrix correlations), you can use its p-value to back-calculate a standard error.
You may also see rcalc suggested for non-independent correlations. It’s meant for a different problem: several correlations measured on the same individuals (see 2.3). It doesn’t fix the non-independence of dyads within a single matrix.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
NoteKey points





\(Z_r\) is the Fisher’s z transformation of Pearson’s \(r\). Only Pearson’s r goes into escalc directly; convert other correlation types first.
Many \(Z_r\) type data presentation formats include error bars. These can create issues with unit of replication. Data reconstruction techniques are possible but should be used with caution
Other data types include relationships between continuous predictors and discrete responses, which require care but can be estimated with \(Z_r\) and converted to lnOR
Calculating \(Z_r\) from non-independent correlation data, such as from pairwise matrices, requires additional care but is also described in detail.
\(Z_r\) describes correlations between a continuous predictor variable and a (generally) continuous response variable. \(Z_r\) is thus an important effect size in the meta-analyst tool kit, especially with observational data.
\(Z_r\) type data often takes the form of a scatterplot but other formats exist (e.g., matrices, time series, and model estimates). We’ll go through these examples in turn, along with solutions and limitations for extracting \(Z_r\) type data. We’ll start, however, by describing how to structure a database for \(Z_r\) type effect sizes.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
Database design
In general, \(Z_r\) effect size extractions require a long-format database for data entry, where each row is one of the points in the corresponding analysis. This is because you will most likely be extracting individual points from scatterplot figures, instead of directly reported correlation coefficients (\(r\)).
This dataset will then be summarized in R to derive \(r\) (using cor.test) and sample size (\(n\)), producing a derived dataset with a single row per unique correlation. Be sure to have clear ID columns to help with summarization. Alternatively, you can calculate \(r\) and \(n\) while extracting data but this may lead to clunkiness in your workflow.
Note that some studies (though rarely in our experience) will report the raw correlation coefficients (\(r\)) and sample size (\(n\)), which will require a simpler data entry format (1 row per correlation coefficient). These can be entered into the same raw dataset or into a separate tab.






ImportantTypes of directly reported correlations



The \(Z_r\) effect size is based on a transformation of Pearson’s correlation coefficient (\(r\)). However, there are other correlation types. Spearman correlation is used for non-parametric correlation tests, Kendall for XXXXX, biserial for an artificially discretized predictor variable, and point-biserial for a truly discretized predictor variable.
Of these, it appears that all but point-biserial can be used to calculate \(Z_r\) without adjustment (Jacobs and Viechtbauer 2017). escalc has measure arguments directly designed to convert biserial correlations to \(Z_r\) (measure = "ZBIS").


Your dataset may look like this, with the first correlation (corr_1) represented as raw data extracted from a scatterplot and the second correlation (corr_2) entered directly as the correlation coefficient and sample size:

This will then be summarized in R to calculate the correlation coefficient \(r\) and sample size. We offer a helper function get_r that allows you to do this more succinctly:

get_r <- function(x, y){
  out <- cor.test(x, y)
  return(out$estimate)
}

# Summarize the raw correlation data:
dat.summarized <- dat %>%
  filter(!is.na(x)) %>%
  group_by(correlation_id) %>%
  summarize(r = get_r(x, y),
            n = n())

# Bind with the already summarized correlation data:
dat.final <- rbind(dat.summarized,
                   dat %>% 
                     filter(!is.na(r)) %>%
                     select(-x, -y))

# Now calculate Zr:
dat.summarized <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR",
                         ri = r, ni = n,
                         data = dat.final)

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
Simple figures
This is the simplest type of correlation figure. In this case, you’d calibrate the x and y axes and extract each point. Then use cor.test in R to calculate the correlation coefficient:







Figure 1— Simulated scatter of 50 points (grey) with a least-squares line. Each point is one observation, so n = 50. There are no error bars.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
Overplotting
But what if there is an ugly cluster of overlapping points?







Figure 2— Simulated scatter of 50 points (grey). The pink points are 11 copies of one point (row 5) jittered to show an overplotted cluster of 12 observations at one location. There are no error bars.




If the total number of points is reported for the study, you can duplicate the values of the pink points as many times as it takes to match the total sample size. Otherwise, you’ll just have to digitize as many as you can and use a sample size that may be less than the real sample size (which makes the overall \(Z_r\) estimate more conservative—e.g., less weight in the model).
In the figure above, we could safely eyeball 5 separate points (though in reality there are 12).

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
Single axis error bars
But what do you do if each point is actually a mean±SD?







Figure 3— Mean y ± SD for each site (grey points, error bars show ±1 SD), with a least-squares line through the site means. Each point is one site; the internal sample size per site is 10 measurements.




Let’s imagine that each point is a site. Most researchers likely ignore the \(SD\) and calculate \(Z_r\) from the site means and number of sites, as follows:

head(dat)

          x         y        sd     n
      <num>     <num>     <num> <num>
1: 7.441598  9.669735 0.2781988    10
2: 6.715727  9.514692 0.3842851    10
3: 6.629420  7.743130 0.2887549    10
4: 8.008286 10.638801 0.4780718    10
5: 7.384331 10.704274 0.4863912    10
6: 6.768715  8.675752 0.2815391    10

out_site <- cor.test(dat$x, dat$y)
site_mean_estimates <- escalc(measure = "ZCOR",
                               ri = out_site$estimate,
                               ni = nrow(dat))
site_mean_estimates


      yi     vi 
1 1.3248 0.0213 


However, calculating \(Z_r\) this way treats site as the unit of replication. If the other studies in your dataset also treat site as the unit of replication, this is the best approach. However, if the rest of your data uses individuals or plots as the unit of replication you will end up with misaligned units of replication.
An alternative approach is to simulate the underlying data behind each site-level summary (i.e., the points in the scatterplot above). This can help align the units of replication with your dataset and ensure that studies with higher effort have more influence in your models. To do so:

Determine the internal sample size of each point, i.e., how many measurements were summarized to produce the means ± error.
Extract the means and error and convert error to \(SD\)
Use these statistics to draw random samples of of the data underlying each point from the appropriate statistical distribution (with the length of this sample equal to the internal sample size).

Note that this process can align the unit of replication of this data with the rest of your dataset. However, it also introduces a different issue: the individual observations are not equally independent (i.e., they’re clustered within each point). Luckily, there is a way to correct for this, which we’ll demonstrate below.
Here we’ll use rnorm to draw normally distributed data for each point. Note that it is also possible to draw data from other distributions (see here and here for a worked example with a \(Z_r\)-type effect size and the binomial distribution)






Warning



Note that reconstructing underlying data is an experimental method. Use carefully.


The first few rows of our extracted data looks like this, with an internal sample size of 10 measurements per site:

                                          sd = dat$sd[i],

Warning



If the author-provided data presents standard error (or confidence intervals, etc) instead of standard deviation, remember that you absolutely must convert these to standard deviation before attempting to reconstruct the underlying distribution. See here on how to convert from other measures of error to standard deviation.


If you were to plot this reconstructed data, it would look like this:








In this example, each point had an internal sample size of 10 measurements. The reconstructed dataset therefore has 500 rows (50 sites times 10 measurements), but these rows are not fully independent. All measurements within a site share the site’s x value and the associated spatial or temporal clustering.
So how do we deal with the non-independence among these simulated observations?
We shrink the sample size with a design effect (see here) by calculating the intraclass correlation (ICC). This describes the amount of variation between sites rather than within sites. We estimate it from the scatter of the site means around the regression line and from the within-site SDs:

out <- cor.test(y_expanded$x, y_expanded$y)

fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = dat)
s2_w <- mean(dat$sd^2)                                    # within-site variance
s2_b <- max(var(resid(fit)) - s2_w / mean(dat$n), 0)      # between-site variance
icc <- s2_b / (s2_b + s2_w)
n_eff <- nrow(y_expanded) / (1 + (mean(dat$n) - 1) * icc) # effective n

n_eff

[1] 58.738


The effective sample size became 59—much closer to the number of sites (50) than the total number of observations (500). If the standard deviations around each point had been larger, then effective sample size would be larger and further approach the number of individual measurements.
To calculate \(Z_r\), we calculate \(r\) from the expanded x and y variables:

# Now calculate 'r':
out <- cor.test(y_expanded$x, y_expanded$y)
r <- out$estimate
r

      cor 
0.8424061 


But instead of using 500 as our sample size in our call to escalc, we use our estimate of effective sample size:

escalc(measure = "ZCOR",
       ri = out$estimate,
       ni = n_eff)


      yi     vi 
1 1.2294 0.0179 


Compare this to our site-level \(Z_r\) estimates (n=50), that ignored the error bars:

site_mean_estimates


      yi     vi 
1 1.3248 0.0213 


You can see that sampling variance decreased and the point estimate shifted. You’ll also notice that in this example, the overall influence of simulating the underlying data had only minor influence on our estimates. Take that as you will. Regardless we think this is pretty neat.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
section: x and y axis error bars
text:
x and y axis error bars
What do you do if there are also error bars on the x axis? For example, if each point is a mean±SD of two different measurements. This is common in field studies, where researchers may sample vegetation at a site and some other factor (e.g., animal activity or soil nutrients) and then present the means±SD of each site in a correlation.







Figure 4— Mean y (vertical error bars, ±SD) against mean x (horizontal error bars, ±SD) for all 50 sites. Each point is one site, so the correlation below is an ecological (aggregate) correlation with n = 50 sites.




In this case, the safest bet is likely to use the data as is, tagging the unit of replication as being site-level instead of measurement-level.
However, it is possible to simulate the data underlying these bivariate distributions (bivariate in that they concern correlated x and y measurements). This is, as above, an experimental data reconstruction technique. Use this only if your data is limited and you think it’s essential to glean as much data as possible.

Click here to see a full demonstration
In the table below, you’ll see the extracted mean values for the x and y variables (x, y), their standard deviations (x_sd, y_sd), and their internal sample sizes (x_n and y_n), which differ. To draw from a bivariate distribution we need to use a single sample size. To be conservative, we’ll use whichever sample size is smallest. We’ll then use mvrnorm in the R package MASS.

library("MASS")

head(dat)

          x         y      y_sd   y_n       x_sd   x_n
      <num>     <num>     <num> <num>      <num> <num>
1: 7.441598  9.669735 0.2781988    10 0.16709662    20
2: 6.715727  9.514692 0.3842851    10 0.07276391    20
3: 6.629420  7.743130 0.2887549    10 0.11669007    20
4: 8.008286 10.638801 0.4780718    10 0.20335793    20
5: 7.384331 10.704274 0.4863912    10 0.21119052    20
6: 6.768715  8.675752 0.2815391    10 0.05556844    20

# Choose the n with the lowest sample size:
dat[, n := min(c(x_n, y_n))]

# Specify `rho`, the correlation between x and y:
r <- 0.5

xy_expanded <- list()

for(i in 1:nrow(dat)){
  # Create the correlation matrix between x and y:
  sig <- matrix(
                c(dat$x_sd[i]^2,
                  r * dat$x_sd[i] * dat$y_sd[i],
                  r * dat$x_sd[i] * dat$y_sd[i],
                  dat$y_sd[i]^2),
                nrow = 2, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE
              )
  
  # Draw from the multivariate normal distribution
  xy_expanded[[i]] <- mvrnorm(n = dat$n[i], 
                              mu = c(x = dat$x[i], 
                                     y = dat$y[i]), 
                              Sigma = sig) |>
    as.data.frame()
}
xy_expanded <- rbindlist(xy_expanded)

Our dataset went from 50 rows (one per point in the figure above) to 500 rows, given an internal N of 10 per point.
One issue with this approach is that, in ecology at least, it’s unlikely that the two bivariate distributions are the same. One might be a Beta distribution and the other negative binomial, etc. The normal distribution is unlikely to be the true data generating process (as assumed above).
However, if you do take this approach, the next step would be to calculate ICC and effective sample size (as above). And, as always, conduct sensitivity analyses!

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
Mismatched time series
However, what do you do if the time series are mismatched?
Below, we’ll plot two time series, one for Variable 1 and one for Variable 2:







Figure 6— Two mismatched time series. Variable 1 is sampled yearly (left panel) and Variable 2 is sampled every quarter year (right panel). These are simulated values to show the alignment problem.




What is the best way to line up variable 1 and variable 2 to calculate their correlation? While imputing the missing values in the second panel is one possible approach, it is the least conservative.
Instead, we recommend taking the average of the most frequently sampled variable to align with the less frequently sampled variable. Alternatively, you can filter the data (after aligning by the shared x-axis) to just those occassions where there is data for both series.
Aligning the data like this is tricky and will probably require manual merging based on nearest value in a spreadsheet software (e.g., Excel) after calibrating both the x and y axes.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
section: Discrete responses with a continuous predictor
text:
Discrete responses with a continuous predictor
Imagine you are conducting a meta-analysis concerned with factors driving nest success or failure in a seabird. Many of the studies use a discrete predictor, e.g., presence or absence of a predator. These types of data are naturally suited for lnOR or lnRR effect sizes.
However, other studies report mortality in relationship to the abundance of that predator—e.g., the continuous manifestation of presence/absence.







Figure 7— Simulated nest outcome (1 = fledged, 0 = failed) against predator abundance, one point per nest. The probability of fledging declines with abundance. Points are jittered vertically; n is given in the text.




Depending on your meta-analysis question you may want to extract this data and calculate a \(Z_r\) correlation effect size, which can then be converted to lnOR (see here) and compared to your other lnOR discrete-predictor effect sizes. To do so, extract each point, which is an individual, and calculate \(Z_r\) with the responses as a binary variable of 0 or 1.
This conversion is safe because presence/absence is a discretized version of abundance and because the unit of replication is the number of nests (or individuals) in both cases and the conversion formulas assume that discrete variables are discretized or extreme ends of a continuous variable (which is true with presence and absence).
Regardless, care is still necessary. It’s unclear the extent to which calculating \(Z_r\) on binary outcomes can estimate the estimand of lnOR. A potentially safer option is to extract the raw data and fit a logistic regression of nest fate on predator abundance. The coefficient is the lnOR per unit of abundance. However, it’s unclear whether this can be compared to other lnOR’s in your dataset. This was an idea from Santi but I’m not sure it’s comparable.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
section: Proportion data with a continuous predictor
text:
Proportion data with a continuous predictor
You can imagine similar challenges where instead of 0 or 1 responses, the authors report % of a population:







Figure 8— Proportion alive (y axis, a population-level summary) against temperature (degrees C), at nine temperature treatments. The proportion declines monotonically; there are no error bars.




You can calculate \(Z_r\) directly between the predictor (temperature, x-axis) and the proportion alive (the y axis), directly.
However, each location on the x-axis actually represents a population of individuals, all of whom were monitored to determine the proportion alive. As such, simply calculating \(Z_r\) directly from the proportion ignores population size and treats the number of surveys (or sites) as the unit of replication (n=10).
This can lead to a serious mismatch with the rest of your dataset—if the rest of your dataset is based the number of individuals as the unit of replication (like above)
To deal with this, the best option would be to convert the proportion data to binary response data based on the total number of individuals in each x-axis treatment—if this can be reconstructed from author reported summaries.
For example, if this figure reflects an experiment where each temperature treatment had 15 individuals, then you can multiply the survivorship at each temperature level by 15, and then expand this dataset to have a 0 or 1 for all 15 individuals per temperature treatment. Because each count is deterministic (rounded from the proportion), there is no added random noise.
Let’s give it a try. dt is a data.table with a column for proportion alive and for temperature. We’ll calculate the number of living and dead individuals, make the dataset long so that these are in one column, and then duplicate the dataset to be one row per individual. Finally, we’ll create a binary column of 0s and 1s:

dt[, number_alive := floor(proportion_alive * 15)]
dt[, number_dead := 15 - number_alive]
head(dt)

   temperature proportion_alive number_alive number_dead
         <num>            <num>        <num>       <num>
1:        10.0        0.8175745           12           3
2:        12.5        0.7057850           10           5
3:        15.0        0.5621765            8           7
4:        17.5        0.4073334            6           9
5:        20.0        0.2689414            4          11
6:        22.5        0.1645165            2          13

# Now melt dataset:
dt.mlt <- melt(dt, 
               measure.vars = c("number_alive", "number_dead"),
               variable.name = "status", 
               value.name = "n_individuals")
head(dt.mlt)

   temperature proportion_alive       status n_individuals
         <num>            <num>       <fctr>         <num>
1:        10.0        0.8175745 number_alive            12
2:        12.5        0.7057850 number_alive            10
3:        15.0        0.5621765 number_alive             8
4:        17.5        0.4073334 number_alive             6
5:        20.0        0.2689414 number_alive             4
6:        22.5        0.1645165 number_alive             2

# Now expand dataset to a binary response dataset:
dt.expanded <- dt.mlt[rep(seq_len(.N), n_individuals), ]
dt.expanded$n_individuals <- NULL

# Add binary column:
dt.expanded[, living := ifelse(status == "number_alive", 1, 0)]
dt.expanded$status <- NULL

We have now expanded this dataset from 9 rows (one per temperature treatment) to 135 rows (one per individual), and we have shifted the unit of replication from number of temperature treatments to number of individuals.
We can now calculate a correlation coefficient and \(Z_r\) effect size:

res <- cor.test(dt.expanded$living, dt.expanded$temperature)

escalc(measure = "ZCOR",
       ni = nrow(dt.expanded),
       ri = res$estimate) |> unlist() 

          yi           vi 
-0.679413208  0.007575758 


This can be converted to lnOR for comparability. Note that since the individuals within each temperature treatment might be correlated, treat this reconstruction with some degree of caution and be sure that this data does not unduly influence your results.

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
section: Mean±SD proportion data with continuous predictor {#sec-\(Z_r\)-reconstructing-proportion-data}
text:
Mean±SD proportion data with continuous predictor {#sec-\(Z_r\)-reconstructing-proportion-data}
Now let’s look at a similar situation, except the figure is presenting mean±SD mortality across separate trials within each temperature treatment.







Figure 9— Mean proportion alive (points) ± SD (error bars) across trials within each of five temperature treatments. Each trial has 20 individuals and there are 3 trials per treatment (n = 60 individuals per treatment).




The default in this situation is to calculate \(Z_r\) on the treatment means, with a site/experiment level unit of replication, with n equal to the number of temperature treatments (5). This may be difficult to compare to effect sizes (presumably lnOR) calculated with individual-level unit of replication.






Note



This may be a situation that calls single-group effect sizes that use temperature as a moderator in a metaregression. See our page here.


However, if we want our unit of replication to be based on the number of individuals, we could alternatively reconstruct the underlying distributions behind each of these summarized trials. This will allow us to calculate a correlation across individuals for the binary response of being alive or dead, instead of across the mean per trial.






Note



A similar data structure could occur with discrete outcomes per plot instead of individuals with the number of sites/islands interchangeable with the number of trials.
An example would be the number of plots occupied by a species (the discrete outcome) per study site (the trial), which are sampled across some continuous gradient of interest.


To do this, we use the binomial or beta-binomial distribution instead of the normal distribution. The design effect (see 3.3) corrects the sample size for the clustering of individuals within trials. To do so we need to determine, from the text, the number of individuals and the number of trials (or sites, plots, etc) that the mean±sd were calculated from.






Note



A similar data structure could occur with discrete outcomes per plot instead of individuals with the number of sites/islands interchangeable with the number of trials.
An example would be the number of plots occupied by a species (the discrete outcome) per study site (the trial), which are sampled across some continuous gradient of interest.


Since this type of data reconstruction is experimental, use with caution, flag, and conduct sensitivity analyses.

Click here for a full demonstration
To understand whether to use the binomial or beta-binomial distribution, we check whether the observed (author-reported) standard deviation is greater than the theoretical standard deviation of the binomial distribution, which is defined by the proportion and the number of individuals per trial.

theoretical_sd <- sqrt((dt$proportion_alive * (1 - dt$proportion_alive))/(dt$n_individuals))

nrow(dt[sd > theoretical_sd])

[1] 0


It looks like the reported standard deviations are all less than or equal to the theoretical standard deviation of the binomial family. So we can use the binomial distribution. Here we use fixed (deterministic) counts rather than random draws: the number alive in each treatment is round(proportion_alive * N), where N is the total number of individuals in that treatment (n_individuals * n_trials). W
hy not random draws? They add simulation noise about as large as the sampling error itself, and they give a different answer every time you run the code. See here for the equations and a fuller description, as well as how to generate data for beta-binomial distributed data (when \(sd_{reported} > sd_{theoretical}\)).






Warning



Note that reconstructing underlying data is an experimental method. Use carefully.



dt[, n_total := n_individuals * n_trials]                 # individuals per treatment
dt[, n_alive := round(proportion_alive * n_total)]        # deterministic counts
dt[, n_dead := n_total - n_alive]

# Design effect from the reported SD (within-trial clustering), floored at 0:
dt[, rho := pmax((n_individuals * sd^2 / (proportion_alive * (1 - proportion_alive)) - 1) /
                   (n_individuals - 1), 0)]
dt[, deff := 1 + (n_individuals - 1) * rho]
dt[, .(temperature, n_total, n_alive, n_dead, rho, deff)]

   temperature n_total n_alive n_dead   rho  deff
         <num>   <num>   <num>  <num> <num> <num>
1:          10      60      42     18     0     1
2:          15      60      39     21     0     1
3:          20      60      24     36     0     1
4:          25      60      23     37     0     1
5:          30      60      16     44     0     1


Now we expand the counts to one row per individual with a binary outcome of living or dead:

long <- melt(dt,
             id.vars = "temperature",
             measure.vars = c("n_alive", "n_dead"),
             variable.name = "status",
             value.name = "count")
long[, living := as.integer(status == "n_alive")]

final_dat <- long[rep(seq_len(nrow(long)), long$count), .(temperature, living)]

nrow(final_dat)

                   tail(final_dat, 5)))

res <- cor.test(final_dat$living, final_dat$temperature)

escalc(measure = "ZCOR",
       ri = res$estimate,
       ni = nrow(final_dat) / mean(dt$deff))


       yi     vi
