title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
text:
Matrices
Some types of correlations are more complicated because they are based on pairwise matrices that describe relationships between individuals. As such, each value is not independent because the same individuals engaged with other individuals.
For instance, correlations between pair-wise behaviors. An example would be the relationship between grooming behavior and defense, which was meta-analyzed by Schino (2007). Is grooming adaptive because it leads to mutual defense with grooming partners?
With data like this, you might have a directed matrix of grooming between individuals, and a second matrix of defense between the same individuals. Here we simulate 10 individuals, with defense correlated with grooming:

n_ind <- 10
groom <- matrix(runif(n_ind^2, min = 1, max = 100), nrow = n_ind)
diag(groom) <- NA

defend <- groom + matrix(rnorm(n_ind^2, mean = 0, sd = 15), nrow = n_ind)
diag(defend) <- NA

knitr::kable(round(groom[1:4, 1:4], 1))



NA
14.6
94.1
86.6


36.2
NA
83.7
16.0


41.7
30.6
NA
59.2


8.2
82.2
24.7
NA




Each off-diagonal cell is a directed dyad. Because the grooming matrix is directed, we use both triangles, so every off-diagonal value enters the calculation. We melt the two matrices into vectors of aligned dyads:

keep <- !is.na(groom)
dyads <- data.table(grooming = groom[keep], defence = defend[keep])
nrow(dyads)

[1] 90


Now calculate Kendall’s correlation across the dyads and convert it to a Pearson-equivalent r with \(r = \sin(\pi\tau/2)\) before calculating Zr. The sample size is the number of individuals, not the number of dyads:

tau <- cor(dyads$grooming, dyads$defence, method = "kendall")
r_matrix <- sin(pi * tau / 2)

escalc(measure = "ZCOR",
       ri = r_matrix,
       ni = n_ind)


      yi     vi 
1 1.4650 0.1429 


The dyads share individuals, so they are not independent, and the standard error above is only a first approximation. If the paper reports a Mantel or QAP test (permutation tests built for matrix correlations), you can use its p-value to back-calculate a standard error.
You may also see rcalc suggested for non-independent correlations. It’s meant for a different problem: several correlations measured on the same individuals (see 2.3). It doesn’t fix the non-independence of dyads within a single matrix.

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Calculating lnOR
Let’s calculate lnOR for our example data with escalc in metafor:

# Calculate lnOR for each experiment with escalc
dat_or <- escalc(measure = "OR",
                 ai = ai, bi = bi,
                 ci = ci, di = di,
                 data = dat_dichotomous)
dat_or


       site ai bi ci di     yi     vi 
1 Wetland A 15 85 10 90 0.4626 0.1895 
2 Wetland B 20 30 15 35 0.4418 0.1786

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Interpreting lnOR
To interpret lnOR (including a pooled model estimate ± confidence intervals), exponentiate it (\(e^{lnOR}\)) to convert it back to an OR. Let’s take our

or_a <- exp(dat_or$yi[1])
round(or_a, 1)

[1] 1.6




OR = 1: Equal odds of the event in both groups (e.g., the stressor has no effect on the odds of infection).

OR > 1: Higher odds of the event in the exposed group.

OR < 1: Lower odds of the event in the exposed group.

There are several ways to describe an OR of 1.59 in plain English, which are more or less comfortable based on whether OR is ≥ 1 or < 1.

If OR is ≥ 1, convert to percent change, using \(100 \times (OR - 1)\):


The odds of infection were 59% higher in the exposed group than in the control group.


You can also write in terms of multiples by rounding the odds ratio:


The exposed group had 1.59 times the odds of infection of the control group.


If the OR value is < 1, it might be easier to write from the control group’s perspective, using \(1/OR\):


The control group had 0.63 times the odds of infection than the exposed group.


Similarly, when the OR is below 1, you can use \(100 \times (1 - OR)\) to get the percentage decrease.


The control group had -58.82% reduction in the odds of infection.

Avoid describing an OR as “times more likely”: that describes risk, not odds (see Choosing an effect size).






NoteClick to understand why odds are not risk





Halving the odds is not the same as halving the risk. The change in risk depends on the baseline risk, \(p_0\), which is the risk in the control group. Given an OR and a baseline risk, the risk in the exposed group is:
\[p_1 = \frac{OR \times p_0}{1 - p_0 + OR \times p_0}\]
The table below shows an OR of 0.5 at three different baseline risks:




Baseline (control) risk
Risk in exposed group
Risk ratio (RR)



5%
2.6%
0.51


30%
17.6%
0.59


60%
42.9%
0.71





With a 5% baseline risk, an OR of 0.5 lowers the risk from 5% to 2.6%, a relative drop of about the same size as the drop in odds. With a 60% baseline risk, the same OR only lowers the risk from 60% to 42.9%, an RR of 0.71.

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Sampling variance
Variance for the OR is calculated on a natural logarithmic scale:
\[
Var(lnOR) = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} + \frac{1}{d}
\tag{3}\]

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Continuity correction
As you can see in Equation 2 and Equation 3, if any cell (\(a\), \(b\), \(c\), or \(d\)) is 0 (e.g., no individuals were infected in the control group), lnOR and its variance can’t be calculated (\(\frac{x}{0}=\infty\). By default, escalc() adds 0.5 to every cell of any table that contains a 0:

escalc(measure = "OR",
       ai = 10, bi = 10,
       ci = 0, di = 5)


      yi     vi 
1 2.3979 2.3723 


If there are no events (or only events) in both groups, the study gives no information about the OR and should be left out (higgins2024?). You can do this by adding drop00 = TRUE in escalc() or you can manually exclude those data points.
We discuss other methods for rare events and many 0 cells below.

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Calculating lnRR

dat_rr <- escalc(measure = "RR", 
                 ai = ai, bi = bi, 
                 ci = ci, di = di, 
                 data = dat_dichotomous)
dat_rr


       site ai bi ci di     yi     vi 
1 Wetland A 15 85 10 90 0.4055 0.1467 
2 Wetland B 20 30 15 35 0.2877 0.0767

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Interpreting lnRR
To interpret these effect sizes (and the final model estimates), you first convert lnRR to RR by exponentiating (\(e^{lnRR}\)):

rr_a <- exp(dat_rr$yi[1])
rr_a

[1] 1.5


For Experiment 1, the lnRR is 0.405, which is an RR of 1.5.
Interpret RR as follows:

RR = 1: Equal risk (or probability) between the comparison groups (e.g., a stressor has no effect on overall mortality risk).
RR > 1: Higher risk (or probability) of the event in the exposed group.
RR < 1: Lower risk (or probability) of the event in the exposed group.

In plain English, you can write the RR for Experiment 1 in two ways:
There are two ways to describe an RR of 1.5 in plain English:

Subtract 1 from the RR and multiply by 100 to get the relative change in risk: \(100 \times (RR - 1)\). A positive value means higher risk in the exposed group, and a negative value means lower risk. When RR is below 1, \(100 \times (1 - RR)\) is called the Relative Risk Reduction.


The outcome is 50% more likely in the exposed group than in the control group.

When the RR is below 1, use \(100 \times (1 - RR)\) to get the percentage decrease. This is called the relative risk reduction.

You can also report the RR directly, which is easier to interpret than the OR.


The exposed group was 1.5 times as likely to experience the outcome as the control group.







Note



Notice that the OR for Wetland A (1.59) is further from 1 than the RR (1.5). This gap grows as the event becomes more common.

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Sampling variance
Like lnOR, lnRR variance is calculated on the log scale:
\[
Var(lnRR) = \frac{1}{a} - \frac{1}{a + b} + \frac{1}{c} - \frac{1}{c + d}
\tag{6}\]

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Continuity correction
lnRR breaks down when \(a\) or \(c\) equals 0, so it also needs a continuity correction. Like lnOR, escalc adds 0.5 to all four cells of the affected table, not only the affected group, so \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) each increase by 1. The same advice about studies with no events in either group applies here: set drop00 = TRUE unless you have a good reason to keep them.






ImportantDefining the target event



You must clearly define your target event. It is easy to accidentally swap success with failure, or fledged with failed. Switching the target event (analyzing non-events instead of events) affects each effect size differently:

OR: The new estimate becomes the exact reciprocal (\(1/x\)). In the 30% baseline example above, a mortality OR of 0.5 becomes a survival OR of 2.
RR: The estimate changes and is not simply the reciprocal. Its precision and significance can also change, sometimes substantially, which is a troubling mathematical property of RR. In the same 30% example, the mortality RR is 0.59, but the survival RR is 1.18.

Best practice: Define the less common outcome as the target event. This reduces errors and heterogeneity between studies (higgins2024?). Give your columns informative names to reduce data entry errors and utilize reproducible, trackable extraction practices, such as provided by the R package metaDigitise. We also recommend color-coding your columns in your spreadsheet to reduce confusion.

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Calculating RD

dat_rd <- escalc(measure = "RD", 
                 ai = ai, bi = bi, 
                 ci = ci, di = di, 
                 data = dat_dichotomous)
dat_rd


       site ai bi ci di     yi     vi 
1 Wetland A 15 85 10 90 0.0500 0.0022 
2 Wetland B 20 30 15 35 0.1000 0.0090

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Interpreting RD


RD = 0: Equal risk of the event in both groups.

RD > 0: Higher risk of the event in the exposed group.

RD < 0: Lower risk of the event in the exposed group (also called the absolute risk reduction).


rd_a <- dat_rd$yi[1]

In plain English, the RD of 0.05 for Wetland A can be written as:

Infection was 5 percentage points higher in the exposed group than in the control group (5 more infected individuals per 100).

Note the difference from the RR: infection was 50% more likely in the exposed group (relative change), but only 5 percentage points higher (absolute change).

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Sampling variance
Because the RD is not log transformed, its variance is calculated on the raw scale:
\[
Var(RD) = \frac{a \times b}{(a + b)^3} + \frac{c \times d}{(c + d)^3}
\tag{8}\]






ImportantDefining the target event



You must clearly define your target event. It is easy to accidentally swap success with failure, or fledged with failed. Switching the target event (analyzing non-events instead of events) affects each effect size differently:


lnOR: The sign flips (the OR becomes its reciprocal, \(1/OR\)).

RD: The sign flips.

lnRR: The estimate, its precision, and its statistical significance can all change, in ways that are hard to predict (higgins2024?).

Best practice: Define the less common outcome as the target event. This reduces errors and heterogeneity between studies (higgins2024?). Give your columns informative names to reduce data entry errors. We also recommend color-coding your columns in your spreadsheet to reduce confusion.

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
section: Applied ecological examples: matching the effect size to your study design
text:
Applied ecological examples: matching the effect size to your study design
Which effect size you use depends on two things: what your study design lets you calculate, and what you want to say about the result.
Example 1: You can’t calculate the proportion of each group that experienced the event → OR only
Example: Testing whether large horns protect beetles from bird predation. Researchers collect the remains of killed beetles (cases) and sample living beetles from the same area (controls), then compare how common large horns are in each group.
Why only the OR?
The researchers choose how many killed and living beetles to collect. If they collect 100 of each, half the sample is “killed”, whatever the real predation rate is. So the data can’t tell us the risk of being killed, and the RR and RD can’t be calculated. The OR still works because it gives the same answer whether you compare horn size between killed and living beetles, or compare survival between large- and small-horned beetles.
Example 2: You can calculate the proportions and want to say how many times higher or lower the risk is → RR
Example: A two-year experiment tracking 1,000 oak seedlings inside deer exclosures and 1,000 in open plots, with mortality as the target event.
Why the RR?
Every seedling is counted at planting, so we know the true risk of dying in each treatment. If 35% die in open plots and 14% in exclosures, the RR is 0.40: exclosures cut mortality risk by 60%. The OR for the same data is 0.30, which readers could mistake for a 70% cut. When an event is common, the OR makes the effect look bigger than it is.
Example 3: You can calculate the proportions and want to say how many more or fewer events occurred → RD alongside RR
Example: Comparing butterfly colonization between isolated habitat fragments and fragments linked by a corridor: 20% of isolated and 35% of connected patches are colonized over the study period.
Why add the RD?
The RR (1.75) says connected patches are 75% more likely to be colonized. The RD (0.15) says how many extra patches that is: about 15 per 100 connected, or one extra colonization for roughly every 7 patches connected. The same RR could mean a much smaller gain if colonization were rarer (4% vs. 7% is still an RR of 1.75, but only 3 extra patches per 100). The RD is what you need to judge whether corridors are worth the cost.

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Comparing the three effect sizes









Effect size
What it compares
Scale
Main strength
Main limitation



OR
Odds between groups
Relative
Works for case-control designs and matches logistic regression
Less intuitive and can exaggerate relative effects for common events


RR
Risk between groups
Relative
Direct and intuitive interpretation
Requires known risks and is capped by baseline risk


RD
Difference in risk
Absolute
Directly communicates ecological impact
Less comparable across populations with different baseline risks



In short:


OR vs. RR: Both describe relative effects, but the OR is based on odds and the RR on risk. They are approximately equal only when the event is rare.

RR vs. RD: Both are based on risk, but the RR describes proportional change while the RD describes absolute change.

OR vs. RD: The OR describes relative change on the odds scale, whereas the RD describes absolute change. The same OR can produce very different RDs depending on baseline risk.

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
What time-to-event data look like
A 2×2 table only records whether each individual had the event. Time-to-event data also record when. At the individual level, each row is one individual, with how long it was followed and whether the event happened:


Nest
Group
Days followed
Event



1
Fenced
12

2
Fenced
30
0 (survived to end of study)


3
Unfenced
5

4
Unfenced

Rows with a 0 are censored: we know the nest survived at least that long, but not what happened after.
Summed by group, the closest match to the 2×2 table at the top of this page is:










Events
Censored
Total
Total time at risk



Exposed (e.g., Fenced)
a
b
a + b
\(T_1\)


Control (e.g., Unfenced)

\(T_2\)



The new column, total time at risk, is the days followed added up across all individuals in the group. Dividing events by time at risk gives an event rate for each group (\(a/T_1\) and \(c/T_2\)), and the ratio of the two rates estimates the hazard ratio (introduced below):
\[
HR \approx \frac{a / T_1}{c / T_2}
\]
This is the same calculation as the incidence rate ratio in Multiple events per individual, so you can use escalc(measure = "IRR") with x1i = a, x2i = c, t1i = T1, and t2i = T2.
The catch is that this only gives the true HR if the hazard stays roughly constant over the study. If risk changes over time (e.g., nest predation peaks at hatching), the summary table loses that information, and an HR from a Cox model or log-rank test will be more accurate. Papers also rarely report total time at risk, so in practice you’ll usually extract a reported HR instead (see Getting hazard ratios from studies).






ImportantDon’t use mean time-to-event



It can be tempting to compare average survival time between groups, as you would for any continuous outcome (e.g., with lnRR or SMD). Don’t. You can only measure survival time for individuals that had the event during the study. Those still alive at the end don’t have a death date, so they get left out. Leaving them out skews the average, because the individuals left out are the ones that lived longest.
For example, if a study ends after 30 days, every animal that survived past day 30 is missing from the average. The group that survived best loses the most animals from the calculation, so the comparison can make it look worse than it is.

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
The hazard ratio
The standard effect size for time-to-event data is the hazard ratio (HR). The hazard is the risk of the event happening at a given moment, among individuals that haven’t experienced it yet. The HR compares this between groups:


HR = 1: The event happens at the same rate in both groups.

HR > 1: The event happens sooner (or more often at any given time) in the exposed group.

HR < 1: The event happens later (or less often at any given time) in the exposed group.

Most analyses assume the HR stays constant over the study period, even if the hazard itself rises and falls (e.g., nest predation peaks at hatching). This is called the proportional hazards assumption. If the effect clearly changes over time (e.g., a treatment protects seedlings in the first month but not after), a single HR can be misleading.
As with the OR and RR, HRs are log transformed for meta-analysis.
In plain English, an HR of 0.60 for nest predation in fenced vs. unfenced plots means:

At any point during the nesting period, nests in fenced plots were predated at 60% of the rate of nests in unfenced plots (a 40% lower hazard).

Note that this is not the same as “40% fewer nests were predated”. The HR describes the rate at which events happen, not the final proportion.

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Getting hazard ratios from studies
escalc() can’t calculate HRs from summary data, because an HR needs the individual survival times. The ideal is to obtain the raw data from study authors and reanalyze it yourself, so every study is analyzed the same way. In practice, you will usually have to work from what the papers report, which often isn’t the statistic you need (higgins2024?).
There are three ways to get an HR from a published study. For practical, step-by-step guidance on all three, see (tierney2007?).
1. Extract the reported HR and its uncertainty. Studies that use a Cox proportional hazards model (or another survival regression) report an HR, usually with a 95% CI. You can convert these to lnHR and its standard error:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&lnHR = \ln(HR) \\
&SE(lnHR) = \frac{\ln(CI_{upper}) - \ln(CI_{lower})}{3.92}
\end{aligned}
\]

# Hazard ratios for nest predation (fenced vs. unfenced) from two studies
dat_hr <- data.frame(
  study = c("Study A", "Study B"),
  hr = c(0.62, 0.80),
  ci_lb = c(0.41, 0.55),
  ci_ub = c(0.94, 1.16)
)

dat_hr <- dat_hr %>%
  mutate(yi = log(hr),
         sei = (log(ci_ub) - log(ci_lb)) / (2 * qnorm(0.975)),
         vi = sei^2)

If a study reports an HR with an exact P value but no CI, you can recover the standard error from the P value (higgins2024?):
\[
SE(lnHR) = \frac{|lnHR|}{z}, \qquad z = \Phi^{-1}(1 - P/2)
\]

# e.g., HR = 0.70, P = 0.03
abs(log(0.70)) / qnorm(1 - 0.03 / 2)

[1] 0.1643595


This only works with exact P values. “P < 0.05” or “NS” doesn’t give you enough information.
2. Estimate it from a log-rank test. Many studies compare survival curves with a log-rank test rather than a Cox model. If you know the observed number of events in the exposed group (O), the number expected if the exposure had no effect (E), and the variance of the log-rank statistic (V), then (simmonds2011?):
\[
lnHR \approx \frac{O - E}{V}, \qquad SE(lnHR) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{V}}
\]
This is the same calculation as the Peto odds ratio, applied to survival data. Studies rarely report O, E, and V directly, but they can often be worked out from the reported P value, the number of events in each group, and the survival curves (parmar1998?; williamson2002?). These methods involve several assumptions, so it’s worth involving a statistician.
The same calculation can be done on grouped data. For example, a nest study might report how many nests were predated each week and how many were still active at the end of each week. A log-rank analysis of these counts gives O, E, and V, but because the data are grouped, the HR is only approximate (this grouped estimate is sometimes called a log odds ratio in older literature, e.g., (ebctcg1990?)). Censored individuals need careful handling, and when the intervals are long relative to the study (e.g., yearly checks in a three-year study), methods for interval-censored survival are more appropriate (collett1994?).
3. Reconstruct it from a Kaplan–Meier curve. If a study only shows a survival curve, you can digitize the curve and reconstruct approximate individual data (guyot2012?). This lets you estimate the HR yourself, and also opens up other analyses of the survival data. It takes more work, so it’s best kept for studies that can’t be included any other way.

title: Effect Sizes for Dichotomous Data: Assumptions and Interpretation
text:
Converting to a 2×2 table instead
If every individual was followed for at least a fixed time (say 30 days), and studies report how many in each group had experienced the event by then, you can build a 2×2 table and use lnOR, lnRR, or RD as usual. This only works if no individuals were censored before that time point. It also throws away information about when events happened, so it’s best used when most studies report outcomes this way.
Don’t mix HRs with ORs or RRs in the same meta-analysis. They measure different things and only give similar values when events are rare.

title: Rates of change
text:
\(Z_r\) effect sizes describe both the direction and strength (i.e., tightness) of a relationship between two continuous variables. As we demonstrated in the \(Z_r\) section, this means that relationships with identical slopes can vary dramatically in their \(Z_r\) coefficients:

Codelibrary("ggplot2")

set.seed(42)
n <- 50
x <- rnorm(n)
e <- as.numeric(scale(resid(lm(rnorm(n) ~ x))))  # noise uncorrelated with x, so the fitted slope equals b exactly
scenarios <- data.frame(
  panel = c("A. Steep slope, little scatter", "B. Steep slope, lots of scatter", "C. Shallow slope, little scatter"),
  b     = c(1, 1, 0.2),
  sigma = c(0.4, 2, 0.08)
)

sim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(scenarios)), function(i) {
  data.frame(panel = scenarios$panel[i], x = x,
             y = scenarios$b[i] * x + scenarios$sigma[i] * e)
}))

labs_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(sim, sim$panel), function(d) {
  data.frame(panel = d$panel[1],
             label = sprintf("slope = %.2f\nr = %.2f\nZr = %.2f", 
                             coef(lm(y ~ x, data = d))[2], 
                             cor(d$x, d$y),
                             atanh(cor(d$x, d$y))))
}))

p <- ggplot(sim, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "hotpink", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = labs_df, aes(x = -1.5, y = 4, label = label),
            # hjust = -0.1, 
            vjust = 1.2, size = 3.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 12))+
  labs(x = "Predictor (x)", y = "Response (y)")
p






Figure 1— Three simulated datasets with the same 50 values of \(x\). Panels A and B share the same slope but differ in scatter, so their correlations differ. Panels A and C have very different slopes but the same scatter relative to the slope, so their correlations are identical.




However, sometimes you might only be interested in the slope of a relationship and you want the sampling variance estimate to absorb the noise as a weight in your models.
For example, imagine you want to calculate individual species abundance trajectories through time to ask which species are declining and which are increasing.
You’re not interested in the strength of the relationship of each species with time but in the slope itself. This is because you know full well that the relationship with time will be noisy: each year is wetter or drier, etc. Instead, you’re interested in which species are winning and which are losing (and, using metaregression, why).
As Fig. 1, illustrates, identical correlation coefficients (panels A and C) can have radically different slopes while identical slopes can have radically different correlations (panels A and B).
In these cases, you can meta-analyze regression coefficients from linear models or S-statistics from non-parametric Mann-Kendall tests, along with their model estimated standard errors (after transforming to sampling variance with \(Var = SE^2\)). Using these effect sizes is not common and we do not discuss these effect sizes in depth.
However, see Daufresne et al. (2009) and Pilotto et al. (2020) for meta-analyses using S-statistics to analyze time series data. Note that because of temporal autocorrelation, you may want to see Hamed and Ramachandra Rao (1998) for adjusted calculation of sampling variance.
We do suggest that if you do conduct a meta-analysis on these regression coefficients, that you might want to pair this with a meta-analysis on \(Z_r\), to capture the noisiness of the relationships between your response and predictor variables.
Assumptions
Using regression slopes or S-statistics is more dangerous than the other effect sizes we have covered in this tutorial. Ideally you would calculate these slopes from raw data, either extracted from scatter plots or from the article’s supplementary material or large synthesized databases (e.g., BioTime Dornelas et al. (2025)).
This is because slopes are sensitive to the units of both the predictor and the response variables. As such, using author-reported model estimates is not advised unless the units were identical between studies and all models contained the same predictors (also in the same units). This is unlikely.
After calculating model-derived slopes (or S-statistics), convert the model-derived standard errors (\(se\)) to sampling variance (\(Var = se^2\)) and fit your meta-analytic model. It is critical that the regression coefficients are derived from identical response and predictor variables, which are in the same units across all of the effect sizes.
If you must use author provided model estimates, with models that varied in the response and predictor units, then you are back in the world of correlations, which describe both slope and strength of a relationship. The effect sizes for these model-derived estimates are Fisher’s r-to-z transformed correlation coefficient (see measure = "ZPCOR" in escalc’s documentation and here). Note that these must be estimates from linear models, without random effects.






ImportantMaybe just fit a GLMM on raw data



Analyzing regression coefficients requires raw data, because regression coefficients will change based on the units of the variables. Likewise, regression coefficients will change based on the number of moderators in a model (and random effects). As such, these should not be extracted from author-reported model summaries (unless the models are identical across studies).
If you have the raw data, you might want to consider just fitting generalized linear mixed effect models, using random effect structures to control for non-independence between the different data sources.
The only reason you might not want to use a GLMM is that the estimates for each individual observation (e.g., a species through time) will shrink towards the global mean, which may conceal the patterns you’re interested in uncovering.

title: Variability between groups
text:
PASTED TOGETHER CONTENT FROM SEPARATE PAGES. NOT EDITED
The most commonly used effect sizes concern mean relationships between variables.
However, variability is itself a meaningful dimension of reality, not merely noise (Nakagawa et al. 2026). In ecological contexts, heterogeneity is considered a key driver of biodiversity and ecosystem functioning (Stein et al. 2014, Levine et al. 2016). Likewise, in evolution, variability tells us important information about selective pressures which can either increase variation (Buckley and Huey 2016, O’Dea et al. 2016) or reduce it (Crispo 2007).
There are two main effect sizes for calculating variability between two groups (i.e., discrete predictors): lnVR and lnCVR (Nakagawa et al. 2015).

title: Variability between groups
text:
lnVR
lnVR is the log-transformed ratio of the standard deviations of two groups:
\[
\mathrm{lnVR}=\ln\left(\frac{sd_1}{sd_2}\right),
\tag{1}\]
where \(sd_1\) is the treatment-group standard deviation and \(sd_2\) is the control-group standard deviation. If group 1 is your treatment or experimental group:

\(\mathrm{lnVR}>0\): the treatment group is more variable than the control group;
\(\mathrm{lnVR}=0\): the groups have equal standard deviations;
\(\mathrm{lnVR}<0\): the treatment group is less variable.

Interpretation
lnVR can be back transformed to plain english by exponentiating (i.e., \(e^{lnVR}\)).
If we have an lnVR of 0.4: \(e^{0.4}\approx1.5\). This indicates that the standard deviation of the treatment group is approximately 50% higher than the control group.
Combining an lnRoM or SMD meta-analysis of mean differences with an lnVR meta-analysis can provide a more complete biological description of biological change.
How to calculate
To calculate lnVR, use measure="VR" in escalc:

escalc(measure = "VR",
       sd1i = 3, n1i = 20,
       sd2i = 2, n2i = 20)


      yi     vi 
1 0.4055 0.0526 


There is a paired version of lnVR as well, which requires an estimate of the correlation between group 1 and 2, which we can specify as 0.5 or 0.8 if it’s unreported (which is typical, see here). Use this formula if groups 1 and 2 are paired, e.g., from paired plots, before-after experiments, and so on.
In escalc this is specified with the “VRC” measure:

escalc(measure = "VRC",
       sd1i = 1.5, sd2i = 2.5,
       ni = 15, ri = 0.5)







Note



Senior et al. (2026) recently demonstrated that using bivariate models with lnRoM and lnVR as response variables can increase statistical power to detect effects of treatments on both variation and mean responses. This is an interesting and little implemented method to incorporate both mean differences and variability into a single meta-analytic model.

title: Variability between groups
text:
lnCVR
lnCVR is the log-transformed coefficient of variation ratio. Its definition formula (prior to small sample bias correction) is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
lnCVR=\ln\left(\frac{s_1/m_1}{s_2/m_2}\right)
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]
This effect size is standardized by the mean. As such, this effect size cannot accept negative mean values, requiring positive, ratio-scale data like the lnRoM effect size. (Note that standard devations can never be negative so lnVR is always calculable as long as standard deviations were reported, even if means are <0).
Importantly, lnCVR describes both mean differences between groups and differences in variability and has an exact mathematical relationship with lnVR and lnRoM:
\[
lnCVR = lnVR - lnRoM
\tag{3}\]






Important



Because lnCVR is defined by both lnVR and lnRoM, we recommend analyzing both lnVR and lnRoM (or SMD) separately instead of using lnCVR for most meta-analyses. Together, they will describe both differences in variability and differences in mean relationships.


lnCVR is intended to account for a common biological pattern: groups with larger means often also have larger variances. However, dividing by the mean makes an implicit scaling assumption. In simple terms, it works most naturally when the standard deviation increases roughly in proportion to the mean. Equivalently, variance then increases roughly with the square of the mean.
That relationship differs among data types:

Approximately normal data with constant variance: the standard deviation may stay similar as the mean changes. The coefficient of variation will then change mechanically with the mean.
Poisson count data: variance equals the mean, so standard deviation increases with the square root of the mean rather than directly with the mean. The coefficient of variation therefore decreases as the mean increases.
Negative-binomial count data: variance can increase much faster than the mean. At large means, the standard deviation may be close to proportional to the mean, but the relationship depends on the dispersion parameter.
Proportions and other bounded responses: variance is constrained by the mean and commonly shrinks near the boundaries. The mean–variance relationship can therefore be strong and nonlinear.

For these reasons, do not choose lnCVR automatically. First plot or model the relationship between group means and standard deviations across the dataset. Use lnCVR when relative variability is the intended estimand and its assumed mean–variance scaling is plausible. In all cases, we recommend using both lnVR and lnCVR, as well as lnRoM or SMD. If the results are different, these sensitivity analyses can help you understand why.
How to calculate
This can be calculated in escalc with measure = "CVR". This effect size requires the same statistical ingredients as SMD and lnRoM:

escalc(measure = "CVR",
       m1i = 15, m2i = 15,
       sd1i = 1.5, sd2i = 2.5,
       n1i = 15, n2i = 15)

There is a paired version of lnCVR as well. In escalc this is specified with measure="CVRC".

escalc(measure = "CVRC",
        m1i = 15, m2i = 15,
       sd1i = 1.5, sd2i = 2.5,
       ni = 15, ri = 0.5)

title: Extracting \(Z_r\): the correlation coefficient
section: Mean±SD proportion data with continuous predictor {#sec-\(Z_r\)-reconstructing-proportion-data}
text:
Mean±SD proportion data with continuous predictor {#sec-\(Z_r\)-reconstructing-proportion-data}
Now let’s look at a similar situation, except the figure is presenting mean±SD mortality across separate trials within each temperature treatment.







Figure 9— Mean proportion alive (points) ± SD (error bars) across trials within each of five temperature treatments. Each trial has 20 individuals and there are 3 trials per treatment (n = 60 individuals per treatment).




The default in this situation is to calculate \(Z_r\) on the treatment means, with a site/experiment level unit of replication, with n equal to the number of temperature treatments (5). This may be difficult to compare to effect sizes (presumably lnOR) calculated with individual-level unit of replication.






Note



This may be a situation that calls single-group effect sizes that use temperature as a moderator in a metaregression. See our page here.


However, if we want our unit of replication to be based on the number of individuals, we could alternatively reconstruct the underlying distributions behind each of these summarized trials. This will allow us to calculate a correlation across individuals for the binary response of being alive or dead, instead of across the mean per trial.






Note



A similar data structure could occur with discrete outcomes per plot instead of individuals with the number of sites/islands interchangeable with the number of trials.
An example would be the number of plots occupied by a species (the discrete outcome) per study site (the trial), which are sampled across some continuous gradient of interest.


To do this, we use the binomial or beta-binomial distribution instead of the normal distribution. The design effect (see 3.3) corrects the sample size for the clustering of individuals within trials. To do so we need to determine, from the text, the number of individuals and the number of trials (or sites, plots, etc) that the mean±sd were calculated from.






Note



A similar data structure could occur with discrete outcomes per plot instead of individuals with the number of sites/islands interchangeable with the number of trials.
An example would be the number of plots occupied by a species (the discrete outcome) per study site (the trial), which are sampled across some continuous gradient of interest.


Since this type of data reconstruction is experimental, use with caution, flag, and conduct sensitivity analyses.

Click here for a full demonstration
To understand whether to use the binomial or beta-binomial distribution, we check whether the observed (author-reported) standard deviation is greater than the theoretical standard deviation of the binomial distribution, which is defined by the proportion and the number of individuals per trial.

theoretical_sd <- sqrt((dt$proportion_alive * (1 - dt$proportion_alive))/(dt$n_individuals))

nrow(dt[sd > theoretical_sd])

[1] 0


It looks like the reported standard deviations are all less than or equal to the theoretical standard deviation of the binomial family. So we can use the binomial distribution. Here we use fixed (deterministic) counts rather than random draws: the number alive in each treatment is round(proportion_alive * N), where N is the total number of individuals in that treatment (n_individuals * n_trials). W
hy not random draws? They add simulation noise about as large as the sampling error itself, and they give a different answer every time you run the code. See here for the equations and a fuller description, as well as how to generate data for beta-binomial distributed data (when \(sd_{reported} > sd_{theoretical}\)).






Warning



Note that reconstructing underlying data is an experimental method. Use carefully.



dt[, n_total := n_individuals * n_trials]                 # individuals per treatment
dt[, n_alive := round(proportion_alive * n_total)]        # deterministic counts
dt[, n_dead := n_total - n_alive]

# Design effect from the reported SD (within-trial clustering), floored at 0:
dt[, rho := pmax((n_individuals * sd^2 / (proportion_alive * (1 - proportion_alive)) - 1) /
                   (n_individuals - 1), 0)]
dt[, deff := 1 + (n_individuals - 1) * rho]
dt[, .(temperature, n_total, n_alive, n_dead, rho, deff)]

Now we expand the counts to one row per individual with a binary outcome of living or dead:

long <- melt(dt,
             id.vars = "temperature",
             measure.vars = c("n_alive", "n_dead"),
             variable.name = "status",
             value.name = "count")
long[, living := as.integer(status == "n_alive")]

final_dat <- long[rep(seq_len(nrow(long)), long$count), .(temperature, living)]

nrow(final_dat)

This final dataset has 300 rows, one for each individual, with number of individuals as the nominal unit of replication. Because individuals within a trial are correlated, we divide the sample size by the mean design effect (1) before calculating Zr:

res <- cor.test(final_dat$living, final_dat$temperature)

escalc(measure = "ZCOR",
       ri = res$estimate,
       ni = nrow(final_dat) / mean(dt$deff))
